nodes.name: Definitional equivalence of HF and PA
nodes.statement: Additionally, \cite{swierczkowski2003finite} proves that HF and PA are definitionally equivalent, i.e. each of HF and PA is an extension of the other. More specifically, if one adds the binary relation symbol and the binary function symbol of HF to PA, then the axioms of HF can be proved in PA. The analogous converse is also true.
assumptions: if one adds the binary relation symbol and the binary function symbol of HF to PA
conclusions: HF and PA are definitionally equivalent
then the axioms of HF can be proved in PA
nodes.statement_short: HF and PA are definitionally equivalent: each is an extension of the other.

nodes.name: Language of HF
nodes.statement: The \textit{first-order language of HF}, denoted by $\mathcal{L}$, has an alphabet of \textit{symbols} given by the logical constants $=$, $\lor$, $\neg$, $\exists$, the variables denoted by lower case Latin letters, one binary relation symbol $\in$, one binary function symbol $\lhd$, and one constant symbol $\varnothing$. The connectives $\land$, $\rightarrow$, $\leftrightarrow$, and $\forall$ are considered abbreviations.
nodes.statement_short: The language $\mathcal{L}$: logical symbols, variables, relation $\in$, function $\lhd$, constant $\varnothing$.
nodes.label: def:Lang

nodes.name: Term of L
nodes.statement: It follows that any \textit{term} of $\mathcal{L}$ arises in the following way: any variable is a term, any constant symbol is a term, and if $\sigma, \tau$ are terms, then so is $\sigma \lhd \tau$.

nodes.name: L-formula
nodes.statement: Furthermore, any \textit{$\mathcal{L}$-formula} arises in the following way: any atomic formula is an $\mathcal{L}$-formula, and if $\varphi, \psi$ are $\mathcal{L}$-formulas, then so are $\neg \varphi$, $\varphi \lor \psi$, and $\exists x \varphi$.

nodes.name: Axioms of HF
nodes.statement: The \textit{axioms of HF} are the following $\mathcal{L}$-formulas: \begin{enumerate} \item $z=\varnothing \leftrightarrow \forall x(x \notin z)$. \item $z=x \lhd y \leftrightarrow \forall u(u \in z \leftrightarrow u \in x \lor u=y)$. \item $(\alpha(\varnothing) \land \forall x \forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]) \rightarrow \forall x \alpha(x)$, \end{enumerate} where $\alpha$ is any $\mathcal{L}$-formula which contains a distinguished freely occurring variable $z$ such that $x$ and $y$ are substitutable for $z$.
nodes.statement_short: HF axioms: empty set, adjunction $x\lhd y$, and the $\in$-induction scheme.
also_stated_at: $z=x \lhd y \leftrightarrow \forall u(u \in z \leftrightarrow u \in x \lor u=y)$.

The assumption in Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom} is that $\alpha$ is any $\mathcal{L}$-formula which contains a distinguished freely occurring variable $z$ such that $x$ and $y$ are substitutable for $z$.
nodes.label: def:Axioms

nodes.name: Sentential (Boolean) axioms
nodes.statement: For any $\mathcal{L}$-formulas $\varphi, \psi, \mu$: $$ \begin{aligned} \varphi & \rightarrow \varphi, \\ \varphi & \rightarrow \varphi \lor \psi, \\ \varphi \lor \varphi & \rightarrow \varphi, \\ \varphi \lor(\psi \lor \mu) & \rightarrow(\varphi \lor \psi) \lor \mu, \\ (\varphi \lor \psi) \land(\neg \varphi \lor \mu) & \rightarrow \psi \lor \mu . \end{aligned} $$
nodes.label: def:Bool.Axioms

nodes.name: Specialisation axiom
nodes.statement: For any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$ and every $x_i$: $$\varphi \rightarrow \exists x_i \varphi.$$
nodes.label: def:Spec.Axiom

nodes.name: Equality axioms
nodes.statement: $$ \begin{aligned} x_1 & = x_1, \\ \left(x_1=x_2\right) \land \left(x_3=x_4\right) & \rightarrow \left[\left(x_1=x_3\right) \rightarrow \left(x_2=x_4\right)\right], \\ \left(x_1=x_2\right) \land \left(x_3=x_4\right) & \rightarrow \left[\left(x_1 \in x_3\right) \rightarrow \left(x_2 \in x_4\right)\right], \\ \left(x_1=x_2\right) \land \left(x_3=x_4\right) & \rightarrow \left[x_1 \lhd x_3 = x_2 \lhd x_4 \right]. \end{aligned} $$
nodes.label: def:Equality.Axioms

nodes.name: Deduction rules
nodes.statement: For any $\mathcal{L}$-formulas $\varphi, \psi$: \begin{description} \item \textit{Modus Ponens}: From $\varphi$ and $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$, deduce $\psi$. \item \textit{Substitution}: From $\varphi$, deduce $\varphi[x_i/\tau]$ for any term $\tau$ that is substitutable for $x_i$ in $\varphi$. \item \textit{$\exists$-introduction}: From $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$, deduce $\exists x_i \varphi \rightarrow \psi$ provided $x_i$ does not occur freely in $\psi$. \end{description}
nodes.label: def:Prf.mp+Prf.subst+Prf.exists_intro

nodes.name: Theorem of HF
nodes.statement: An $\mathcal{L}$-formula is a \textit{theorem of HF}, denoted by $\vdash \varphi$, if there is a finite sequence of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas — each of which is an axiom of HF, a logical axiom, or is deduced from previous formulas in the sequence by a deduction rule — terminating with $\varphi$.
differentia: there is a finite sequence of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas — each of which is an axiom of HF, a logical axiom, or is deduced from previous formulas in the sequence by a deduction rule — terminating with $\varphi$
nodes.label: def:Prf

nodes.name: Model, model of HF, validity
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathcal{S}$ is an $\mathcal{L}$-structure and $\varphi$ is an $\mathcal{L}$-formula. If every valuation in $\mathcal{S}$ satisfies $\varphi$, say $\mathcal{S}$ is a \textit{model} of $\varphi$, denoted by $\mathcal{S} \vDash \varphi$. If $\mathcal{S}$ is a model of every axiom of HF, say $\mathcal{S}$ is a \textit{model of HF}. An $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$ is called \textit{valid in HF} if every model of HF is a model of $\varphi$, denoted by $\vDash \varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{S}\vDash\varphi$ if every valuation satisfies $\varphi$; models of HF; validity in HF.
nodes.label: def:models+Model+valid

nodes.name: Soundness and completeness
nodes.statement: Suppose $\varphi$ is an $\mathcal{L}$-formula. Then $\vdash \varphi$ if and only if $\vDash \varphi$.
nodes.label: thm:completeness

nodes.name: Proving theorems of HF semantically
nodes.statement: In other words, the theorems of HF are precisely the $\mathcal{L}$-formulas valid in HF. Thus, to prove $\vdash \varphi$ for any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$, it suffices to show that for an arbitrary model of HF, $\mathcal{S}$, we have $\mathcal{S} \vDash \varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: By completeness, to prove $\vdash\varphi$ it suffices to check $\varphi$ in an arbitrary model of HF.

nodes.name: Singleton, unordered pair and ordered pair
nodes.statement: Abbreviate by $\{x\}$, $\{x,y\}$ and $\langle x,y\rangle$ the following terms: \begin{enumerate} \item $\{x\} = \varnothing \lhd x$. \item $\{x,y\} = \{x\} \lhd y$. \item $\langle x,y\rangle = \{\{x\}, \{x,y\}\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:singleton+pair

nodes.name: Singleton and pair properties
nodes.statement: \leavevmode \begin{enumerate} \item $ u\in \{x\} \leftrightarrow u = x$. \item $u \in \{x,y\}\leftrightarrow u=x \lor u=y$. \item $\{x,x\} = \{x\}$. \item $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle u,v\rangle \leftrightarrow x=u \land y=v$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj

nodes.name: Proof of Singleton and pair properties
nodes.statement: \leavevmode \begin{enumerate} \item This follows directly from Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.3. \item This follows directly from Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2 and Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.1. \item This follows directly from Theorem \ref{thm:exten_prop}, Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.1 and Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.2. \item The proof closely follows an analogous proof from ZF by \cite{enderton1977elements}. The $\leftarrow$ direction is trivial. For the $\rightarrow$ direction, by the definition of ordered pairs, the hypothesis can be rewritten to \begin{equation*} \{\{x\}, \{x,y\}\} = \{\{u\}, \{u,v\}\}. \end{equation*} It follows that \begin{equation} \{x\} \in \{\{u\}, \{u,v\}\}\quad\text{and}\quad \{x,y\} \in \{\{u\}, \{u,v\}\} \end{equation} and similarly \begin{equation} \{u\} \in \{\{x\}, \{x,y\}\}\quad\text{ and }\quad \{u,v\} \in \{\{x\}, \{x,y\}\}. \end{equation} By Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.2, (2) can be rewritten to \begin{equation*} (\textbf{a})\quad\{u\}=\{x\}\quad\text{or}\quad (\textbf{b})\quad\{u\}=\{x,y\} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} (\textbf{c})\quad\{u,v\}=\{x\}\quad\text{or}\quad (\textbf{d})\quad\{u,v\}=\{x,y\}. \end{equation*} Note that, by Theorem \ref{thm:exten_prop}, Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.1 and Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.2, \begin{equation} \forall x \forall y \forall z (\{x,y\} = \{z\} \leftrightarrow x = y =z). \end{equation} Now, consider three cases: \begin{itemize} \item Suppose (\textbf{b}) holds. Then, by (3), $u=x=y$. By Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.3, it then follows that (\textbf{d}) can be rewritten to $\{u,v\}=\{x\}$, implying (\textbf{c}) and (\textbf{d}) are equivalent. Thus, by (3), under (\textbf{b}), it must hold that $u=v=x=y$. \item Suppose (\textbf{c}) holds. Then, by (3), $u=v=x$. Note that, by (1) and Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.2, either $\{x,y\}=\{u\}$ or $\{x,y\}=\{u,v\}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.3, it follows that $\{u,v\}=\{u\}$ and thus these two statements are equivalent. Thus, by (3), under (\textbf{c}), it must hold that $x=y=u=v$. \item Suppose (\textbf{a}) and (\textbf{d}) hold. From (\textbf{a}) we have $u=x$. From (\textbf{d}) it follows that, by Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.2, $v=x$ or $v=y$. In the latter case, $u=x\land v=y$. If $v=x$, then $u=v=x$, and case (\textbf{c}) holds by (3); this case has already been considered. \end{itemize} \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Existence of the union of two sets
nodes.statement: $\exists z \forall u (u \in z \leftrightarrow u \in x \lor u \in y)$.
conclusions: $\exists z \forall u (u \in z \leftrightarrow u \in x \lor u \in y)$.
nodes.label: thm:exists_union

nodes.name: Proof of Existence of the union of two sets
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists z \forall u (u \in z \leftrightarrow u \in x \lor u \in y)$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}. \begin{itemize} \item For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=y$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.1. \item For the induction step — $\forall w[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(w) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd w)]$ — pick $w$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $x \cup y$. By Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2, $\alpha(x \lhd w)$ is equivalent to $\exists z \forall u (u \in z \leftrightarrow u \in x \lor u = w \lor u \in y)$. Then, take $z= (x \cup y) \lhd w$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom; adjoin $w$ to $x\cup y$.

nodes.name: Inductive step: take $z=(x\cup y)\lhd w$

By Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2, $\alpha(x \lhd w)$ is equivalent to $\exists z \forall u (u \in z \leftrightarrow u \in x \lor u = w \lor u \in y)$. Then, take $z= (x \cup y) \lhd w$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2.

nodes.name: Proof of Existence of the union of a set of sets
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists z \forall u (u \in z \leftrightarrow \exists (y\in x)[u \in y])$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}. \begin{itemize} \item For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\varnothing$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.1. \item For the induction step — $\forall w[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(w) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd w)]$ — pick $w$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $\bigcup x$. We need to find $z$ such that \begin{equation*} \begin{split} u \in z & \leftrightarrow \exists (y \in x \lhd w)[u \in y]\\ & \leftrightarrow \exists y[(y \in x \lor y = w) \land u \in y]\\ & \leftrightarrow \exists(y \in x)[u \in y] \lor u \in w\\ & \leftrightarrow u \in \bigcup x \lor u \in w, \end{split} \end{equation*} using Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2. Thus, take $z = (\bigcup x) \cup w$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom; $\bigcup(x\lhd w)=(\bigcup x)\cup w$.

nodes.name: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists z \forall u (u \in z \leftrightarrow \exists (y\in x)[u \in y])$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom.

nodes.name: Base case: take $z=\varnothing$
nodes.statement: For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\varnothing$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.1.

nodes.name: Inductive step: take $z=(\bigcup x)\cup w$
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall w[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(w) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd w)]$ — pick $w$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $\bigcup x$. We need to find $z$ such that \begin{equation*} \begin{split} u \in z & \leftrightarrow \exists (y \in x \lhd w)[u \in y]\\ & \leftrightarrow \exists y[(y \in x \lor y = w) \land u \in y]\\ & \leftrightarrow \exists(y \in x)[u \in y] \lor u \in w\\ & \leftrightarrow u \in \bigcup x \lor u \in w, \end{split} \end{equation*} using Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2. Thus, take $z = (\bigcup x) \cup w$.

nodes.name: Comprehension Scheme
nodes.statement: $\exists z \forall u (u\in z \leftrightarrow (u \in x) \land \varphi (u))$, for any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$ in which $z$ is not free.
assumptions: for any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$ in which $z$ is not free
nodes.label: thm:comp_scheme

nodes.name: Proof of Comprehension Scheme
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists z \forall u (u\in z \leftrightarrow (u \in x) \land \varphi (u))$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}. \begin{itemize} \item For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\varnothing$ and use L emma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.1. \item For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $ \{u \in x : \varphi (u)\}$. We need to find $z$ such that \begin{equation*} \begin{split} u \in z & \leftrightarrow (u \in x \lhd y) \land \varphi (u)\\ & \leftrightarrow (u \in x \lor u = y) \land \varphi (u), \end{split} \end{equation*} using Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2. Since $z$ is not free in $\varphi$, take $z = \{u \in x : \varphi (u)\} \lhd y$ if $\varphi(y)$ and $z=\{u \in x : \varphi (u)\}$ if $\neg \varphi(y)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom; adjoin $y$ iff $\varphi(y)$.

nodes.name: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists z \forall u (u\in z \leftrightarrow (u \in x) \land \varphi (u))$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom.

nodes.name: Base case: take $z=\varnothing$
nodes.statement: For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\varnothing$ and use L emma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.1.

nodes.name: Inductive step: adjoin $y$ or not depending on $\varphi(y)$
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $ \{u \in x : \varphi (u)\}$. We need to find $z$ such that \begin{equation*} \begin{split} u \in z & \leftrightarrow (u \in x \lhd y) \land \varphi (u)\\ & \leftrightarrow (u \in x \lor u = y) \land \varphi (u), \end{split} \end{equation*} using Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2. Since $z$ is not free in $\varphi$, take $z = \{u \in x : \varphi (u)\} \lhd y$ if $\varphi(y)$ and $z=\{u \in x : \varphi (u)\}$ if $\neg \varphi(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: adjoin $y$ or not depending on $\varphi(y)$.

nodes.name: Intersection
nodes.statement: Introduce the notation: \begin{enumerate} \item $x \cap y = \{u \in x : u \in y\}$. \item $\bigcap x = \{u \in \bigcup x : \forall (v \in x)[u \in v] \}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:inter+sInter

nodes.name: Replacement Scheme
nodes.statement: $$[\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)]\rightarrow \exists z \forall v [v\in z \leftrightarrow \exists(u \in x) \psi (u,v)],$$ for any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\psi$ in which $z$ is not free.
assumptions: for any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\psi$ in which $z$ is not free
conclusions: $$[\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)]\rightarrow \exists z \forall v [v\in z \leftrightarrow \exists(u \in x) \psi (u,v)],$$
nodes.label: thm:repl_scheme

nodes.name: Proof of Replacement Scheme
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $[\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)]\rightarrow \exists z \forall v [v\in z \leftrightarrow \exists(u \in x) \psi (u,v)]$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}. \begin{itemize} \item For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\varnothing$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.1. \item For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $\{v : \exists (u\in x)\psi(u,v)\}$ provided that $\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)$. Furthermore, assume $\forall (u \in x \lhd y) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)$, i.e. that $\forall u [(u \in x \lor u = y) \rightarrow \exists! v \psi (u,v)]$. Hence, $\exists! v \psi (y,v)$; let $v_y$ be this unique $v$. Moreover, it follows that $\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)$ and thus $\{v : \exists (u\in x)\psi(u,v)\}$ exists. By Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2, the required $z$ is $\{v : \exists (u\in x)\psi(u,v)\} \lhd v_y$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom; adjoin the unique image of the new element.

nodes.name: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $[\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)]\rightarrow \exists z \forall v [v\in z \leftrightarrow \exists(u \in x) \psi (u,v)]$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom.

nodes.name: Base case: take $z=\varnothing$
nodes.statement: For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\varnothing$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.1.

nodes.name: Inductive step: adjoin the unique image $v_y$ of $y$
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $\{v : \exists (u\in x)\psi(u,v)\}$ provided that $\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)$. Furthermore, assume $\forall (u \in x \lhd y) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)$, i.e. that $\forall u [(u \in x \lor u = y) \rightarrow \exists! v \psi (u,v)]$. Hence, $\exists! v \psi (y,v)$; let $v_y$ be this unique $v$. Moreover, it follows that $\forall (u \in x) [\exists! v] \psi (u,v)$ and thus $\{v : \exists (u\in x)\psi(u,v)\}$ exists. By Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}.2, the required $z$ is $\{v : \exists (u\in x)\psi(u,v)\} \lhd v_y$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: adjoin the unique image $v_y$ of $y$.

nodes.name: Subset relation
nodes.statement: Introduce the abbreviations: \begin{enumerate} \item $y \subseteq x \leftrightarrow \forall v (v\in y \rightarrow v \in x)$. \item $y \subset x \leftrightarrow y \subseteq x \land y \neq x$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:Subset+SSubset

nodes.name: Existence of the power set
nodes.statement: $\exists z \forall u (u\in z \leftrightarrow u \subseteq x).$
nodes.label: thm:exists_powerset

nodes.name: Proof of Existence of the power set
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists z \forall u (u\in z \leftrightarrow u \subseteq x)$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}. \begin{itemize} \item For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\{\varnothing\}$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}, Theorem \ref{thm:exten_prop}, Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.1. \item For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of the power set $P(x)$. One checks directly from the definitions that $$u \subseteq x \lhd y \leftrightarrow u \in P(x) \lor \exists (v \in P(x))[u=v\lhd y].$$ Indeed, for the $\rightarrow$ direction, the cases $y \notin u$ and $y \in u$ correspond to the left and right cases of the disjunction, respectively, where for the right case, the required $v$ is $u \cap x$. The $\leftarrow$ direction is rather trivial. Now, note that the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\psi(v,u): u = v \lhd y$ satisfies the condition for Theorem \ref{thm:repl_scheme}, i.e. $v \mapsto v \lhd y$ is a well-defined mapping. By Theorem \ref{thm:exists_union}, it follows that the required $z$ is $P(x) \cup \{u : \exists (v \in P(x)) [u=v\lhd y]\}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom. The inductive step writes $P(x\lhd y)$ as $P(x)$ union its image under $v\mapsto v\lhd y$, using replacement.

nodes.name: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists z \forall u (u\in z \leftrightarrow u \subseteq x)$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom.

nodes.name: Base case: take $z=\{\varnothing\}$
nodes.statement: For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — take $z=\{\varnothing\}$ and use Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty}, Theorem \ref{thm:exten_prop}, Lemma \ref{lem:mem_singleton+...+pair_inj}.1.

nodes.name: Inductive step: build $P(x\lhd y)$ from $P(x)$ by replacement and union
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of the power set $P(x)$. One checks directly from the definitions that $$u \subseteq x \lhd y \leftrightarrow u \in P(x) \lor \exists (v \in P(x))[u=v\lhd y].$$ Indeed, for the $\rightarrow$ direction, the cases $y \notin u$ and $y \in u$ correspond to the left and right cases of the disjunction, respectively, where for the right case, the required $v$ is $u \cap x$. The $\leftarrow$ direction is rather trivial. Now, note that the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\psi(v,u): u = v \lhd y$ satisfies the condition for Theorem \ref{thm:repl_scheme}, i.e. $v \mapsto v \lhd y$ is a well-defined mapping. By Theorem \ref{thm:exists_union}, it follows that the required $z$ is $P(x) \cup \{u : \exists (v \in P(x)) [u=v\lhd y]\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: build $P(x\lhd y)$ from $P(x)$ by replacement and union.

nodes.name: Assume $P(x)$ exists
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of the power set $P(x)$.

nodes.name: Characterise subsets of $x\lhd y$ via $P(x)$
nodes.statement: One checks directly from the definitions that $$u \subseteq x \lhd y \leftrightarrow u \in P(x) \lor \exists (v \in P(x))[u=v\lhd y].$$

nodes.name: Verify the characterisation by cases $y\notin u$, $y\in u$
nodes.statement: Indeed, for the $\rightarrow$ direction, the cases $y \notin u$ and $y \in u$ correspond to the left and right cases of the disjunction, respectively, where for the right case, the required $v$ is $u \cap x$. The $\leftarrow$ direction is rather trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the characterisation by cases $y\notin u$, $y\in u$.

nodes.name: Replacement applies to $v\mapsto v\lhd y$
nodes.statement: Now, note that the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\psi(v,u): u = v \lhd y$ satisfies the condition for Theorem \ref{thm:repl_scheme}, i.e. $v \mapsto v \lhd y$ is a well-defined mapping.

nodes.name: Union of $P(x)$ and the image gives the power set
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:exists_union}, it follows that the required $z$ is $P(x) \cup \{u : \exists (v \in P(x)) [u=v\lhd y]\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Union of $P(x)$ and the image gives the power set.

nodes.statement: $z\neq \varnothing \rightarrow \exists (w \in z)[w\cap z = \varnothing]$.

nodes.name: Irreflexivity of membership
nodes.statement: $x \notin x$.
nodes.label: cor:mem_irrefl

nodes.name: Proof of Irreflexivity of membership
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem \ref{thm:found_prop} to $z = \{x\}\neq \varnothing$. It follows that $\exists (w \in \{x\})[w\cap \{x\} = \varnothing]$, which implies $x \cap \{x\} = \varnothing$.

nodes.name: Transitive set and ordinal
nodes.statement: We say that $x$ is \textit{transitive} if every element of $x$ is a subset of $x$. We call $x$ an \textit{ordinal} if $x$ is transitive and every element of $x$ is transitive, abbreviated by $\operatorname{Ord}(x)$. Ordinals will be mostly denoted by $k$, $l$, $m$, $n$, $p$, $q$, $r$.
nodes.label: def:IsTrans+IsOrd

nodes.name: Successor
nodes.statement: The \textit{successor} of $x$ is defined as $x \lhd x$, abbreviated by $\operatorname{succ}(x)$.
nodes.label: def:succ

nodes.name: Basic properties of ordinals
nodes.statement: \leavevmode \begin{enumerate} \item $\operatorname{Ord}(k) \rightarrow \operatorname{Ord}(\operatorname{succ}(k))$. \item $\operatorname{Ord}(k) \land l \in k \rightarrow \operatorname{Ord}(l)$. \item $\operatorname{Ord}(\varnothing)$. \item $(\operatorname{Ord}(k) \land (k \neq \varnothing) \land (l \cap k = \varnothing))\rightarrow(l \in k \leftrightarrow l = \varnothing)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:IsOrd.succ_isOrd+...+IsOrd.empty_is_mem

nodes.name: Proof of Basic properties of ordinals
nodes.statement: \leavevmode The proofs of 1, 2 and 3 are immediate from Definitions \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd} and \ref{def:succ}. For 4, assume $k$ is a non-empty ordinal, $l$ is such that $l \cap k = \varnothing$, and suppose $l \in k$. As $k$ is an ordinal, $l \subseteq k$, and as $l \cap k = \varnothing$, it follows that $l=\varnothing$. Conversely, as $k \neq \varnothing$, by Theorem \ref{thm:found_prop} there must exist such an $l \in k$ satisfying $l \cap k = \varnothing$. Hence, $\varnothing \in k$.
nodes.statement_short: Parts 1-3 from definitions; part 4 from transitivity and foundation.

nodes.name: Parts 1-3 are immediate from the definitions
nodes.statement: The proofs of 1, 2 and 3 are immediate from Definitions \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd} and \ref{def:succ}.
nodes.statement_short: Parts 1-3 are immediate from the definitions.

nodes.name: Part 4, forward: $l\in k$ and $l\cap k=\varnothing$ force $l=\varnothing$
nodes.statement: For 4, assume $k$ is a non-empty ordinal, $l$ is such that $l \cap k = \varnothing$, and suppose $l \in k$. As $k$ is an ordinal, $l \subseteq k$, and as $l \cap k = \varnothing$, it follows that $l=\varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: Part 4, forward: $l\in k$ and $l\cap k=\varnothing$ force $l=\varnothing$.

nodes.name: Part 4, backward: foundation gives such an $l\in k$, so $\varnothing\in k$
nodes.statement: Conversely, as $k \neq \varnothing$, by Theorem \ref{thm:found_prop} there must exist such an $l \in k$ satisfying $l \cap k = \varnothing$. Hence, $\varnothing \in k$.
nodes.statement_short: Part 4, backward: foundation gives such an $l\in k$, so $\varnothing\in k$.

nodes.name: Comparability of ordinals
nodes.statement: Let $k,l$ be ordinals. Then, $k \in l \lor k = l \lor l \in k$.

nodes.statement: Clearly, $\neg \beta(k_0,l_0)$. Now suppose, for a contradiction, there exists an ordinal $q_0 \in l_0$ such that $\neg \beta (k_0, q_0)$.

nodes.name: Claim: $l_0\subset k_0$
nodes.statement: We now claim that $l_0 \subset k_0$. Indeed, suppose $p \in l_0$. Then $\beta (k_0, p)$, by (\ref{eq:2}), i.e. $k_0 \in p \lor k_0 = p \lor p \in k_0$. But both $k_0 \in p$ and $k_0 = p$ contradict $\neg \beta(k_0,l_0)$ in (\ref{eq:2}), as $p \in l_0$ is assumed. Thus $p \in k_0$, and $l_0 \subseteq k_0$ follows. Since $l_0 = k_0$ also contradicts $\neg \beta(k_0,l_0)$ in (\ref{eq:2}), we get $l_0 \subset k_0$.

nodes.name: Take $p\in l_0$; by (2) it is comparable with $k_0$
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose $p \in l_0$. Then $\beta (k_0, p)$, by (\ref{eq:2}), i.e. $k_0 \in p \lor k_0 = p \lor p \in k_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $p\in l_0$; by (2) it is comparable with $k_0$.

nodes.statement: But both $k_0 \in p$ and $k_0 = p$ contradict $\neg \beta(k_0,l_0)$ in (\ref{eq:2}), as $p \in l_0$ is assumed. Thus $p \in k_0$, and $l_0 \subseteq k_0$ follows.

nodes.name: Equality is excluded too
nodes.statement: Since $l_0 = k_0$ also contradicts $\neg \beta(k_0,l_0)$ in (\ref{eq:2}), we get $l_0 \subset k_0$.

nodes.name: An $m\in k_0\setminus l_0$ contradicts (1) and (2)

nodes.name: Consequences of comparability of ordinals
nodes.statement: Let $k,l$ be ordinals. Then, \begin{enumerate} \item Exactly one of $k\in l$, $k=l$, $l \in k$ occurs. \item $k\in l \leftrightarrow k \subset l$. \item $l \in k \rightarrow (\operatorname{succ}(l)=k \lor \operatorname{succ}(l)\in k)$. \item $(\operatorname{succ}(k) = \operatorname{succ}(l) )\rightarrow k = l$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: Exactly one of $k\in l$, $k=l$, $l \in k$ occurs.
nodes.label: cor:IsOrd.exclusive_comparability+...+IsOrd.succ_inj

nodes.name: Proof of Consequences of comparability of ordinals
nodes.statement: \leavevmode \begin{enumerate} \item Any two of the three mentioned possibilities contradict Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}. At least one possibility occurs by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}. \item The $\rightarrow$ direction follows by the transitivity of $l$ and Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}. Suppose $k \subset l$. Then $k \in l \lor l \in k$ by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}. But $l \in k$ yields $l \in l$, contradicting Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}. \item By Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}, we have to exclude $k \in \operatorname{succ}(l)$, i.e. we have to show that neither $k\in l$ nor $k=l$ can occur. This is indeed so because each of these possibilities, together with $l\in k$, leads to $l \in l$. \item Suppose, for a contradiction, that $k \neq l$. Then $\operatorname{succ}(k) = k \lhd k = l \lhd l = \operatorname{succ}(l)$ implies $k \in l$ and $l \in k$, yielding again $l \in l$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Each part from comparability and irreflexivity of $\in$.

nodes.name: Part 1 from irreflexivity and comparability
nodes.statement: Any two of the three mentioned possibilities contradict Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}. At least one possibility occurs by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}.

nodes.name: Part 2 from transitivity, comparability and irreflexivity
nodes.statement: The $\rightarrow$ direction follows by the transitivity of $l$ and Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}. Suppose $k \subset l$. Then $k \in l \lor l \in k$ by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}. But $l \in k$ yields $l \in l$, contradicting Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}.
nodes.statement_short: Part 2 from transitivity, comparability and irreflexivity.

nodes.name: Part 3: other alternatives give $l\in l$
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}, we have to exclude $k \in \operatorname{succ}(l)$, i.e. we have to show that neither $k\in l$ nor $k=l$ can occur. This is indeed so because each of these possibilities, together with $l\in k$, leads to $l \in l$.

nodes.name: Part 4: $k\neq l$ gives $l\in l$
nodes.statement: Suppose, for a contradiction, that $k \neq l$. Then $\operatorname{succ}(k) = k \lhd k = l \lhd l = \operatorname{succ}(l)$ implies $k \in l$ and $l \in k$, yielding again $l \in l$.

nodes.name: Order on ordinals
nodes.statement: For ordinals $k,l$, we shall use: \begin{enumerate} \item $k\,<\,l$ to abbreviate $k \in l$, \item $k \leq l$ to abbreviate $k\,<\,l \lor k = l$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:Ord.lt+Ord.le

nodes.name: Ordinals are totally ordered
nodes.statement: On every set of ordinals, the relation $\leq$ ($<$) is a (strict) total order.
conclusions: the relation $\leq$ ($<$) is a (strict) total order.
nodes.label: thm:Ord.le_totalOrder+Ord.lt_sTotalOrder

nodes.name: Proof of Ordinals are totally ordered
nodes.statement: Reflexivity of $\leq$ follows directly from $=$ being reflexive; irreflexivity of $<$ follows directly from Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}. Transitivity is immediate from Definition \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd}. Antisymmetry and asymmetry are straightforward from Definition \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd} and Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}. (Strong) connectivity is derived trivially from Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}.
nodes.statement_short: Check the order axioms using irreflexivity, transitivity and comparability.

nodes.name: (Ir)reflexivity
nodes.statement: Reflexivity of $\leq$ follows directly from $=$ being reflexive; irreflexivity of $<$ follows directly from Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}.

nodes.name: Transitivity from the definition of ordinals
nodes.statement: Transitivity is immediate from Definition \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd}.
nodes.statement_short: Transitivity from the definition of ordinals.

nodes.name: (A)symmetry from definition and irreflexivity
nodes.statement: Antisymmetry and asymmetry are straightforward from Definition \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd} and Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}.

nodes.name: Connectivity from comparability
nodes.statement: (Strong) connectivity is derived trivially from Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.comparability}.

nodes.name: Existence of max and min of a set of ordinals
nodes.statement: If $x$ is a non-empty set of ordinals, then $x$ has a smallest and a largest element, i.e. \begin{equation*} \exists(l \in x) \forall (k \in x) [l \leq k]\quad\text{and}\quad\exists(l \in x) \forall (k \in x) [k \leq l]. \end{equation*}
assumptions: $x$ is a non-empty set of ordinals
conclusions: $x$ has a smallest and a largest element
nodes.label: thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set

nodes.name: Proof of Existence of max and min of a set of ordinals
nodes.statement:
We first prove the existence of the largest element of $x$, denoted by $\max(x)$. Let $\alpha(x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $$( orall (k \in x)[\operatorname{Ord} k]) ightarrow (x 
eq \varnothing) ightarrow (\exists(l \in x)  orall (k \in x) [k \leq l]).$$ We apply Axiom ef{ax:induction_axiom}.  egin{itemize} \item For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — obviously, $x = \varnothing$ immediately contradicts $x 
eq \varnothing$. \item For the induction step — $ orall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) ightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $\max(x)$ if $x$ is a set of ordinals and $x 
eq \varnothing$. Assume $x \lhd y$ is a set of ordinals, evidently non-empty. Then $x$ is a set of ordinals or it is empty. If $x=\varnothing$, then $x \lhd y = \{y\}$, and $\max(x\lhd y) = y$. Now suppose $x 
eq \varnothing$, and thus $\max(x)$ exists. Since $x \lhd y$ arises from $x$ by adjoining one element, it is clear that $\max (x \lhd y)$ also exists. More specifically, it equals $y$ if $\max (x) \in y$, and $\max (x)$ otherwise. \end{itemize} To deduce the existence of $\min (x)$, replace in the above proof $\leq$ by $\geq$ and "max" by "min" throughout.
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom on the set; the minimum follows dually.

nodes.name: Set up induction for the maximum
nodes.statement: We first prove the existence of the largest element of $x$, denoted by $\max(x)$. Let $\alpha(x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $$(\forall (k \in x)[\operatorname{Ord} k]) \rightarrow (x \neq \varnothing) \rightarrow (\exists(l \in x) \forall (k \in x) [k \leq l]).$$ We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction for the maximum.

nodes.name: Base case is vacuous
nodes.statement: For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — obviously, $x = \varnothing$ immediately contradicts $x \neq \varnothing$.

nodes.name: Inductive step: compare $y$ with $\max(x)$
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $\max(x)$ if $x$ is a set of ordinals and $x \neq \varnothing$. Assume $x \lhd y$ is a set of ordinals, evidently non-empty. Then $x$ is a set of ordinals or it is empty. If $x=\varnothing$, then $x \lhd y = \{y\}$, and $\max(x\lhd y) = y$. Now suppose $x \neq \varnothing$, and thus $\max(x)$ exists. Since $x \lhd y$ arises from $x$ by adjoining one element, it is clear that $\max (x \lhd y)$ also exists. More specifically, it equals $y$ if $\max (x) \in y$, and $\max (x)$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Assume the hypothesis for $x$ and that $x\lhd y$ is a set of ordinals
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x)$, i.e. the existence of $\max(x)$ if $x$ is a set of ordinals and $x \neq \varnothing$. Assume $x \lhd y$ is a set of ordinals, evidently non-empty.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the hypothesis for $x$ and that $x\lhd y$ is a set of ordinals.

nodes.name: Case $x=\varnothing$: maximum is $y$
nodes.statement: Then $x$ is a set of ordinals or it is empty. If $x=\varnothing$, then $x \lhd y = \{y\}$, and $\max(x\lhd y) = y$.

nodes.name: Case $x\neq\varnothing$: maximum is $y$ or $\max(x)$
nodes.statement: Now suppose $x \neq \varnothing$, and thus $\max(x)$ exists. Since $x \lhd y$ arises from $x$ by adjoining one element, it is clear that $\max (x \lhd y)$ also exists. More specifically, it equals $y$ if $\max (x) \in y$, and $\max (x)$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Minimum by the dual argument
nodes.statement: To deduce the existence of $\min (x)$, replace in the above proof $\leq$ by $\geq$ and "max" by "min" throughout.

nodes.name: Existence of predecessor
nodes.statement: $(\operatorname{Ord}(k) \land k \neq \varnothing) \rightarrow \exists!l(\operatorname{succ}(l)=k)$.
nodes.label: cor:IsOrd.exists_pred

nodes.name: Proof of Existence of predecessor
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:IsOrd.succ_isOrd+...+IsOrd.empty_is_mem}.2, $k$ is a non-empty set of ordinals. Thus, by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set}, $\max (k)$ exists, where $\max (k) \in k$. It follows from Corollary \ref{cor:IsOrd.exclusive_comparability+...+IsOrd.succ_inj}.3 that either $\operatorname{succ}(\max (k)) = k$ or $\operatorname{succ}(\max (k)) \in k$. However, the latter contradicts the definition of $\max (k)$. Thus $\operatorname{succ}(\max (k)) = k$. Uniqueness follows from Corollary \ref{cor:IsOrd.exclusive_comparability+...+IsOrd.succ_inj}.4.
nodes.statement_short: The predecessor is $\max(k)$; uniqueness by injectivity of successor.

nodes.name: $k$ is a non-empty set of ordinals, so $\max(k)$ exists
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:IsOrd.succ_isOrd+...+IsOrd.empty_is_mem}.2, $k$ is a non-empty set of ordinals. Thus, by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set}, $\max (k)$ exists, where $\max (k) \in k$.
nodes.statement_short: $k$ is a non-empty set of ordinals, so $\max(k)$ exists.

nodes.name: Corollary 2.3 and maximality give $\operatorname{succ}(\max k)=k$
nodes.statement: It follows from Corollary \ref{cor:IsOrd.exclusive_comparability+...+IsOrd.succ_inj}.3 that either $\operatorname{succ}(\max (k)) = k$ or $\operatorname{succ}(\max (k)) \in k$. However, the latter contradicts the definition of $\max (k)$. Thus $\operatorname{succ}(\max (k)) = k$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness by injectivity of succ
nodes.statement: Uniqueness follows from Corollary \ref{cor:IsOrd.exclusive_comparability+...+IsOrd.succ_inj}.4.

nodes.name: Predecessor
nodes.statement: The unique (if existing) $l$ for which $\operatorname{succ}(l) = k$ is called the \textit{predecessor} of $k$, abbreviated by $\operatorname{pred}(k)$.
nodes.label: def:IsOrd.pred

nodes.name: Function and domain
nodes.statement: We say that $x$ is a \textit{function} if every element of $x$ is a an ordered pair and $$ \left(\left\langle u, v_1\right\rangle \in x \wedge\left\langle u, v_2\right\rangle \in x\right) \rightarrow v_1=v_2. $$ Note that $\langle u, v\rangle = \{\{u\}, \{u,v\}\} \in x$ implies $\{u\} \in \bigcup x$, and hence $u \in \bigcup\left(\bigcup x\right)$. Thus, the \textit{domain} of a function $x$ is defined as $$ \operatorname{dom}(x)=\{u \in \bigcup\left(\bigcup x\right): \exists v(\langle u, v\rangle \in x)\} $$ (see Theorems \ref{thm:exists_sUnion} and \ref{thm:comp_scheme}).
nodes.statement_short: A set of ordered pairs that is single-valued; its domain is the set of first components.
nodes.label: def:IsFunc+IsFunc.dom

nodes.name: Sequence
nodes.statement: We call $s$ a \textit{sequence} if $s$ is a function and $\operatorname{dom}(s)=k$ where $k$ is a non-empty ordinal, abbreviated by $\operatorname{Seq}(s,k)$. If $\operatorname{Seq}(s,k)$, then, for any $n\,<\,k$, we write $s_n$ to abbreviate the uniquely existing $z$ such that $\langle n, z\rangle \in s$.
nodes.label: def:IsSeq

nodes.name: Functional formula
nodes.statement: We say an $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$ with $n+1$ free variables is \textit{functional} with respect to a freely occurring variable $y$ if $$ \forall x_1 \ldots \forall x_n \exists! y \varphi (x_1,\ldots, x_n, y). $$
nodes.label: def:IsFunctional

nodes.name: p-function
nodes.statement: If $\varphi$ has $n+1$ free variables and is functional with respect to $y$, we associate with $\varphi$ and $y$ a new $n$-ary function symbol $F_\varphi^y$, called a \textit{p-function}. However, formally, this function symbol is not part of the language $\mathcal{L}$. In particular, $F_\varphi^y(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_n})=u$ abbreviates $$ \exists w (w = u \land \varphi (x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_n},w)), $$ where the latter, in view of $\exists! y \varphi (x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_n},y)$, is equivalent to $\varphi (x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_n},u)$. Examples of \textit{p}-functions are: \begin{itemize} \item $F_\varphi^y(x) = \bigcup x$, with $\varphi(x,y)$ defined as $y = \bigcup x$. \item $F_\psi^y(x) = \bigcap x$, with $\psi(x,y)$ defined as $y = \bigcap x$. \item $F_\chi^y(x) = P (x)$, with $\chi(x,y)$ defined as $y = P (x)$ ($P(x)$ is the power set of $x$). \end{itemize} Often, instead of writing $F_\varphi^y$, we shall use only one capital letter to denote a \textit{p}-function. In the non-arbitrary case, $\varphi$ and $y$ will be specified beforehand.
nodes.statement_short: A formula functional in $y$ yields a defined function symbol $F_\varphi^y$ (an abbreviation outside $\mathcal{L}$).
nodes.label: def:pFunc

nodes.name: Recursion on ordinals
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be an ordinal. Then, for every constant term $\tau$ and \textit{p}-function $G$, there exists a \textit{p}-function $F$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $k=\varnothing \rightarrow F(k) = \tau$. \item $k\neq \varnothing \rightarrow F(k) = G(F(\operatorname{pred}(k)))$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Existence of $p$-functions defined by recursion on ordinals.
nodes.label: thm:Ord.exists_pFuncRecursive

It is easily verified that ef{thm:Ord.exists_pFuncRecursive}.1 and ef{thm:Ord.exists_pFuncRecursive}.2 hold when $F$ is $F_\varphi^y$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\varphi$ via sequences and prove it functional by a least counterexample.

nodes.name: Define $\varphi(k,y)$ via sequences computing the recursion
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi(k,y)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula \begin{equation*} \begin{split} & (k \neq \varnothing \land \exists s [\operatorname{Seq}(s,k) \land y = G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(k)}) \land \forall (n\,<\,k)[(n=\varnothing \land s_n = \tau) \lor\\ &(n \neq \varnothing \land s_n = G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(n)}))]]) \lor (k = \varnothing \land y = \tau). \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\varphi(k,y)$ via sequences computing the recursion.

nodes.statement:
We claim that $\varphi$ is functional with respect to $y$. Indeed, if $k=\varnothing$, then trivially $y=	au$ is unique. Now suppose, for a contradiction, there exists an ordinal $k
eq \varnothing$ such that there is no unique $y$ for which $\varphi(k,y)$. Then, by Theorems ef{thm:comp_scheme} and ef{thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set}, there exists a least ordinal $m
eq\varnothing$ such that there is no unique $y$ for which $\varphi(m,y)$. Let $p=\operatorname{pred}(m)$; it follows there exists a unique $y$ such that $\varphi(p,y)$. Suppose $p
eq \varnothing$. Then there exists $s$ such that  egin{equation*}  egin{split} &\operatorname{Seq}(s,p) \land y = G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(p)}) \land  orall (n\,<\,p)[(n=\varnothing \land s_n = 	au) \lor \& (n 
eq \varnothing \land s_n = G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(n)}))]. \end{split} \end{equation*} But then $	ilde{s} = s \cup \langle p, G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(p)}) angle$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \operatorname{Seq}(	ilde{s},m) \land  orall (n\,<\,m)[(n=\varnothing \land 	ilde{s}_n = 	au) \lor (n 
eq \varnothing \land 	ilde{s}_n = G(	ilde{s}_{\operatorname{pred}(n)}))], \end{equation*} and thus $y = G(	ilde{s}_p)$ uniquely satisfies $\varphi(m,y)$, a contradiction. Now, suppose $p=\varnothing$. Then $ ar{s}=\langle \varnothing, 	au angle$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \operatorname{Seq}( ar{s},m) \land  orall (n\,<\,m)[(n=\varnothing \land  ar{s}_n = 	au) \lor (n 
eq \varnothing \land  ar{s}_n = G( ar{s}_{\operatorname{pred}(n)}))], \end{equation*} and thus $y = G( ar{s}_\varnothing)$ uniquely satisfies $\varphi(m,y)$, again a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $\varphi$ is functional in $y$, by a least counterexample.

nodes.name: Trivial at $\varnothing$; assume a counterexample $k$
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $k=\varnothing$, then trivially $y=\tau$ is unique. Now suppose, for a contradiction, there exists an ordinal $k\neq \varnothing$ such that there is no unique $y$ for which $\varphi(k,y)$.

nodes.name: Take the least counterexample $m$
nodes.statement: Then, by Theorems \ref{thm:comp_scheme} and \ref{thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set}, there exists a least ordinal $m\neq\varnothing$ such that there is no unique $y$ for which $\varphi(m,y)$.

nodes.name: Case $\operatorname{pred}(m)\neq\varnothing$: extend the sequence, contradiction
nodes.statement:
Let $p=\operatorname{pred}(m)$; it follows there exists a unique $y$ such that $\varphi(p,y)$. Suppose $p
eq \varnothing$. Then there exists $s$ such that  egin{equation*}  egin{split} &\operatorname{Seq}(s,p) \land y = G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(p)}) \land  orall (n\,<\,p)[(n=\varnothing \land s_n = 	au) \lor \& (n 
eq \varnothing \land s_n = G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(n)}))]. \end{split} \end{equation*} But then $	ilde{s} = s \cup \langle p, G(s_{\operatorname{pred}(p)}) angle$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \operatorname{Seq}(	ilde{s},m) \land  orall (n\,<\,m)[(n=\varnothing \land 	ilde{s}_n = 	au) \lor (n 
eq \varnothing \land 	ilde{s}_n = G(	ilde{s}_{\operatorname{pred}(n)}))], \end{equation*} and thus $y = G(	ilde{s}_p)$ uniquely satisfies $\varphi(m,y)$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Case $\operatorname{pred}(m)=\varnothing$: one-term sequence, contradiction
nodes.statement: Now, suppose $p=\varnothing$. Then $\bar{s}=\langle \varnothing, \tau \rangle$ satisfies \begin{equation*} \operatorname{Seq}(\bar{s},m) \land \forall (n\,<\,m)[(n=\varnothing \land \bar{s}_n = \tau) \lor (n \neq \varnothing \land \bar{s}_n = G(\bar{s}_{\operatorname{pred}(n)}))], \end{equation*} and thus $y = G(\bar{s}_\varnothing)$ uniquely satisfies $\varphi(m,y)$, again a contradiction.

nodes.name: $F_\varphi^y$ satisfies both recursion clauses
nodes.statement: It is easily verified that \ref{thm:Ord.exists_pFuncRecursive}.1 and \ref{thm:Ord.exists_pFuncRecursive}.2 hold when $F$ is $F_\varphi^y$.

nodes.name: Defined recursively on ordinals
nodes.statement: Say the \textit{p}-function $F$ in Theorem \ref{thm:Ord.exists_pFuncRecursive} is \textit{defined recursively on ordinals}.
nodes.label: def:Ord.pFuncRecursive

nodes.name: Cumulative hierarchy R
nodes.statement: Let $R(x)$ denote the $p$-function defined recursively on ordinals by $$ R(x) = \begin{cases} \varnothing & \text{if } x = \varnothing, \\ P(R(\operatorname{pred}(x))) & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$
nodes.label: def:Ord.R

nodes.name: Monotonicity and transitivity of R
nodes.statement: For all ordinals $m,n$ : \begin{enumerate} \item $n < m \rightarrow R(n) \subset R(m)$. \item $R(m)$ is transitive. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans

nodes.name: Proof of Monotonicity and transitivity of R
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Clearly $R(\varnothing) = \varnothing \subset R(m)$ for all $m>\varnothing$. Now if, for some $m$, there exists some $n<m$ but $R(n) \subseteq R(m)$ fails, then by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set} there is a smallest $n$ with that property. As $n>\varnothing$, it follows that $\operatorname{pred}(n)<\operatorname{pred}(m)$, and thus $R(\operatorname{pred}(n)) \subset R(\operatorname{pred}(m))$. But, by Definition \ref{def:Ord.R}, this implies $R(n) \subset R(m)$, a contradiction. \item Clearly $R(\varnothing) = \varnothing$ is transitive. Now, if $m\neq \varnothing$, then $\operatorname{pred}(m)<m$ and thus $$ x \in R(m) \rightarrow x \subseteq R(\operatorname{pred}(m)) \subset R(m), $$ by Definition \ref{def:Ord.R} and Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.1. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Part 1 by least counterexample; part 2 from the definition and part 1.

nodes.name: Part 1 by a least counterexample
nodes.statement: Clearly $R(\varnothing) = \varnothing \subset R(m)$ for all $m>\varnothing$. Now if, for some $m$, there exists some $n<m$ but $R(n) \subseteq R(m)$ fails, then by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set} there is a smallest $n$ with that property. As $n>\varnothing$, it follows that $\operatorname{pred}(n)<\operatorname{pred}(m)$, and thus $R(\operatorname{pred}(n)) \subset R(\operatorname{pred}(m))$. But, by Definition \ref{def:Ord.R}, this implies $R(n) \subset R(m)$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Take the smallest $n$ violating monotonicity
nodes.statement: Clearly $R(\varnothing) = \varnothing \subset R(m)$ for all $m>\varnothing$. Now if, for some $m$, there exists some $n<m$ but $R(n) \subseteq R(m)$ fails, then by Theorem \ref{thm:IsOrd.exists_max_of_set+IsOrd.exists_min_of_set} there is a smallest $n$ with that property.

nodes.name: Minimality gives the inclusion for predecessors
nodes.statement: As $n>\varnothing$, it follows that $\operatorname{pred}(n)<\operatorname{pred}(m)$, and thus $R(\operatorname{pred}(n)) \subset R(\operatorname{pred}(m))$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives the inclusion for predecessors.

nodes.name: Apply the power set to get a contradiction
nodes.statement: But, by Definition \ref{def:Ord.R}, this implies $R(n) \subset R(m)$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the power set to get a contradiction.

nodes.name: Part 2 from the definition and part 1
nodes.statement: Clearly $R(\varnothing) = \varnothing$ is transitive. Now, if $m\neq \varnothing$, then $\operatorname{pred}(m)<m$ and thus $$ x \in R(m) \rightarrow x \subseteq R(\operatorname{pred}(m)) \subset R(m), $$ by Definition \ref{def:Ord.R} and Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.1.
nodes.statement_short: Part 2 from the definition and part 1.

nodes.name: Every set lies in some R(n)
nodes.statement: $\exists n [\operatorname{Ord}(n) \land x \in R(n)]$.
nodes.label: thm:forall_exists_ord_mem_R

nodes.name: Proof of Every set lies in some R(n)
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists n [\operatorname{Ord}(n) \land x \in R(n)]$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}. \begin{itemize} \item For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — the required ordinal is $\operatorname{succ}(\varnothing)$, as $\varnothing \in P(R(\varnothing)) = P(\varnothing) = \{\varnothing\}$. \item For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y)$, i.e. $x \in R(n)$, $y \in R(m)$ for some ordinals $m,n$. Then, by Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.2, $$ x \lhd y = x \cup \{y\} \subseteq R(n) \cup R(\operatorname{succ}(m)). $$ So, by Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.1, for $k=\max \{\operatorname{succ}(m), n\}$, $x\lhd y \subseteq R(k)$, and thus $x \lhd y \in R(\operatorname{succ}(k))$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom using monotonicity and transitivity of $R$.

nodes.name: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\exists n [\operatorname{Ord}(n) \land x \in R(n)]$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on $x$ via the induction axiom.

nodes.name: Base case: $\varnothing\in R(\operatorname{succ}(\varnothing))$
nodes.statement: For the base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — the required ordinal is $\operatorname{succ}(\varnothing)$, as $\varnothing \in P(R(\varnothing)) = P(\varnothing) = \{\varnothing\}$.

nodes.name: Inductive step: $x\lhd y$ lies in $R$ of a successor
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y)$, i.e. $x \in R(n)$, $y \in R(m)$ for some ordinals $m,n$. Then, by Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.2, $$ x \lhd y = x \cup \{y\} \subseteq R(n) \cup R(\operatorname{succ}(m)). $$ So, by Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.1, for $k=\max \{\operatorname{succ}(m), n\}$, $x\lhd y \subseteq R(k)$, and thus $x \lhd y \in R(\operatorname{succ}(k))$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: $x\lhd y$ lies in $R$ of a successor.

nodes.name: Assume $x\in R(n)$, $y\in R(m)$
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y)$, i.e. $x \in R(n)$, $y \in R(m)$ for some ordinals $m,n$.

nodes.name: Transitivity of $R(m)$ bounds $x\lhd y$
nodes.statement: Then, by Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.2, $$ x \lhd y = x \cup \{y\} \subseteq R(n) \cup R(\operatorname{succ}(m)). $$

nodes.name: Monotonicity gives $x\lhd y\in R(\operatorname{succ}(k))$
nodes.statement: So, by Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}.1, for $k=\max \{\operatorname{succ}(m), n\}$, $x\lhd y \subseteq R(k)$, and thus $x \lhd y \in R(\operatorname{succ}(k))$.

nodes.name: Rank function
nodes.statement: Let $\operatorname{rank}(x)$ denote the least ordinal $n$ such that $x \in R(\operatorname{succ}(n))$, i.e. $x \subseteq R(n)$.
nodes.label: def:rank

nodes.name: Rank increases along membership
nodes.statement: $x \in y \rightarrow \operatorname{rank}(x) < \operatorname{rank}(y)$.
nodes.label: thm:rank.lt_of_mem

nodes.name: Proof of Rank increases along membership
nodes.statement: Let $x \in y$ and suppose $\operatorname{rank}(y)=n$. Then $y \subseteq R(n)$, and thus $x \in R(n)$. It follows that $n \neq \varnothing$ and $x \subseteq R(\operatorname{pred}(n))$. Hence, $\operatorname{rank}(x) \leq \operatorname{pred}(n) < n$.

nodes.name: With $\operatorname{rank}(y)=n$, get $x\in R(n)$
nodes.statement: Let $x \in y$ and suppose $\operatorname{rank}(y)=n$. Then $y \subseteq R(n)$, and thus $x \in R(n)$.

nodes.name: Hence $\operatorname{rank}(x)\le\operatorname{pred}(n)<n$
nodes.statement: It follows that $n \neq \varnothing$ and $x \subseteq R(\operatorname{pred}(n))$. Hence, $\operatorname{rank}(x) \leq \operatorname{pred}(n) < n$.

nodes.name: Transitive closure
nodes.statement: The \textit{transitive closure} of $x$, denoted by $\operatorname{cl}(x)$, is the minimal transitive set $y$ such that $x \subseteq y$.
nodes.label: def:cl

nodes.name: Rank of transitive closure
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{rank}(x) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x))$.
nodes.label: thm:rank_eq_rank_cl

nodes.name: Proof of Rank of transitive closure
nodes.statement: First observe that: \begin{enumerate} \item $u \subseteq v \rightarrow \operatorname{rank}(u) \leq \operatorname{rank}(v)$ (see Definition \ref{def:rank}). \item $\operatorname{rank}(u \cup v) = \max \{\operatorname{rank}(u), \operatorname{rank}(v)\}$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}). \item $\operatorname{rank}(\{w\}) = \operatorname{succ}(\operatorname{rank}(w))$ (see Definition \ref{def:rank}). \end{enumerate} Now, let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\operatorname{rank}(x) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x))$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}. \begin{itemize} \item The base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — is direct as $\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing) = \varnothing$. \item For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y)$, i.e. that for some ordinals $m,n$ we have $\operatorname{rank}(x) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x)) = n$ and $\operatorname{rank}(y) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(y)) = m$. Then both sides on the inclusion $$ x \lhd y = x \cup \{y\} \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x) \cup \operatorname{cl}(y) \cup \{y\} $$ have rank $\max \{n,\operatorname{succ}(m)\}$ (see 2. and 3. above). Since the right hand side is transitive, it follows that $$ x \lhd y \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x \lhd y) \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x) \cup \operatorname{cl}(y) \cup \{y\}, $$ and thus, by 1. above, $\operatorname{rank}(x \lhd y) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x \lhd y))$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction via the HF induction axiom using monotonicity, union and singleton rank facts.

nodes.name: Three auxiliary facts about rank
nodes.statement: First observe that: \begin{enumerate} \item $u \subseteq v \rightarrow \operatorname{rank}(u) \leq \operatorname{rank}(v)$ (see Definition \ref{def:rank}). \item $\operatorname{rank}(u \cup v) = \max \{\operatorname{rank}(u), \operatorname{rank}(v)\}$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}). \item $\operatorname{rank}(\{w\}) = \operatorname{succ}(\operatorname{rank}(w))$ (see Definition \ref{def:rank}).

nodes.name: Rank is monotone under inclusion
nodes.statement: $u \subseteq v \rightarrow \operatorname{rank}(u) \leq \operatorname{rank}(v)$ (see Definition \ref{def:rank}).

nodes.name: Rank of a union is the max
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{rank}(u \cup v) = \max \{\operatorname{rank}(u), \operatorname{rank}(v)\}$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:Ord.R.sSubset_of_lt+Ord.R.isTrans}).
nodes.statement_short: Rank of a union is the max.

nodes.name: Rank of a singleton is the successor
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{rank}(\{w\}) = \operatorname{succ}(\operatorname{rank}(w))$ (see Definition \ref{def:rank}).
nodes.statement_short: Rank of a singleton is the successor.

nodes.name: Set up induction on $x$
nodes.statement: Now, let $\alpha (x)$ be the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\operatorname{rank}(x) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x))$. We apply Axiom \ref{ax:induction_axiom}.

nodes.name: Base case: $\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing)=\varnothing$
nodes.statement: The base case — $\alpha (\varnothing)$ — is direct as $\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing) = \varnothing$.

nodes.name: Inductive step: sandwich $\operatorname{cl}(x\lhd y)$ between sets of equal rank
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y)$, i.e. that for some ordinals $m,n$ we have $\operatorname{rank}(x) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x)) = n$ and $\operatorname{rank}(y) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(y)) = m$. Then both sides on the inclusion $$ x \lhd y = x \cup \{y\} \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x) \cup \operatorname{cl}(y) \cup \{y\} $$ have rank $\max \{n,\operatorname{succ}(m)\}$ (see 2. and 3. above). Since the right hand side is transitive, it follows that $$ x \lhd y \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x \lhd y) \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x) \cup \operatorname{cl}(y) \cup \{y\}, $$ and thus, by 1. above, $\operatorname{rank}(x \lhd y) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x \lhd y))$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: sandwich $\operatorname{cl}(x\lhd y)$ between sets of equal rank.

nodes.name: Assume the hypothesis for $x$ and $y$
nodes.statement: For the induction step — $\forall y[\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y) \rightarrow \alpha(x \lhd y)]$ — pick $y$ arbitrarily and assume $\alpha(x) \land \alpha(y)$, i.e. that for some ordinals $m,n$ we have $\operatorname{rank}(x) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x)) = n$ and $\operatorname{rank}(y) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(y)) = m$.

nodes.name: Both sides of the inclusion have the same rank
nodes.statement: Then both sides on the inclusion $$ x \lhd y = x \cup \{y\} \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x) \cup \operatorname{cl}(y) \cup \{y\} $$ have rank $\max \{n,\operatorname{succ}(m)\}$ (see 2. and 3. above).
nodes.statement_short: Both sides of the inclusion have the same rank.

nodes.name: Transitivity and monotonicity give the claim
nodes.statement: Since the right hand side is transitive, it follows that $$ x \lhd y \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x \lhd y) \subseteq \operatorname{cl}(x) \cup \operatorname{cl}(y) \cup \{y\}, $$ and thus, by 1. above, $\operatorname{rank}(x \lhd y) = \operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{cl}(x \lhd y))$.
nodes.statement_short: Transitivity and monotonicity give the claim.

nodes.name: Restriction
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a function and $z \subseteq \operatorname{dom}(f)$. Then the function $\{y \in f : \exists (u \in z) \exists v (y = \langle u,v \rangle)\}$ will be denoted by $f \upharpoonright z$ and called the \textit{restriction} of $f$ to $z$. Similarly, if $F$ is a \textit{p}-function, then $F \upharpoonright z$ denotes the restriction of $F$ to $z$.
nodes.label: def:IsFunc.restr+pFunc.restr

nodes.name: Recursion on rank
nodes.statement: For every binary $p$-function $G(x,y)$, there exists a unary $p$-function $F$ such that $$ F(x) = G(x, F \upharpoonright \operatorname{cl}(x)). $$
conclusions: there exists a unary $p$-function $F$ such that $$ F(x) = G(x, F \upharpoonright \operatorname{cl}(x)). $$
nodes.label: thm:rank.exists_pFuncRecursive

nodes.name: Proof of Recursion on rank
nodes.statement: For the proof — which is extensive — the reader is referred to Appendix 4 of \cite{swierczkowski2003finite}, where it is presented in detail.

nodes.name: Constant term and length
nodes.statement: The class of \textit{constant terms}, denoted by $\mathbb{C}$, is the class of terms which contain no variables, i.e. $\mathbb{C}$ is the smallest class of terms such that $\varnothing \in \mathbb{C}$ and $\sigma \lhd \tau \in \mathbb{C}$ for any $\sigma, \tau \in \mathbb{C}$. For any $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$, the number of appearances of $\lhd$ in $\tau$ is called the \textit{length} of $\tau$, denoted by $l(\tau)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{C}$: variable-free terms built from $\varnothing$ by $\lhd$; length counts $\lhd$.
nodes.label: def:C+C.length

nodes.name: Finite membership listing for constant terms
nodes.statement: For every non-empty $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$, there are finitely many $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_m \in \mathbb{C}$, all shorter than $\tau$, such that $$ \vdash (x \in \tau \leftrightarrow x = \tau_1 \lor \ldots \lor x = \tau_m). $$
conclusions: there are finitely many $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_m \in \mathbb{C}$, all shorter than $\tau$, such that $$ \vdash (x \in \tau \leftrightarrow x = \tau_1 \lor \ldots \lor x = \tau_m). $$
nodes.statement_short: Every non-empty constant term provably has finitely many shorter constant terms as its members.
nodes.label: lem:C.exists_finset_shorter_and_mem_iff_iSup

nodes.name: Proof of Finite membership listing for constant terms
nodes.statement: We apply induction on the length $l(\tau)$. The case $l(\tau) = 0$, i.e. $\tau = \varnothing$, is trivial. Now assume that the lemma has been established for all non-zero constant terms shorter than $\tau$, and let $\tau$ be $\sigma \lhd \mu$. If $\sigma = \varnothing$, then $\tau = \varnothing \lhd \mu$, where $\mu$ is shorter than $\tau$. We have the theorem of HF $$ \vdash (x \in \varnothing \lhd \mu \leftrightarrow x \in \varnothing \lor x=\mu \leftrightarrow x=\mu), $$ i.e. $m=1$ and $\tau_1 = \mu$. Now suppose $\sigma \neq \varnothing$. As $\sigma$ is shorter than $\tau$, there are $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_n \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $$ \vdash (x \in \sigma \leftrightarrow x=\sigma_1 \lor \ldots \lor x=\sigma_n) $$ Since $\vdash (x \in \tau \leftrightarrow x \in \sigma \lor x=\mu)$, we get $$ \vdash (x \in \tau \leftrightarrow x=\sigma_1 \lor \ldots \lor x=\sigma_n \lor x=\mu). $$ By inductive assumption, each $\sigma_i$ is shorter than $\sigma$, thus also shorter than $\tau$. Also, $\mu$ is shorter than $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the length of the constant term.

nodes.name: Induction on length; base case trivial
nodes.statement: We apply induction on the length $l(\tau)$. The case $l(\tau) = 0$, i.e. $\tau = \varnothing$, is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on length; base case trivial.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis; write $\tau=\sigma\lhd\mu$
nodes.statement: Now assume that the lemma has been established for all non-zero constant terms shorter than $\tau$, and let $\tau$ be $\sigma \lhd \mu$.

nodes.name: Case $\sigma=\varnothing$: one element $\mu$
nodes.statement: If $\sigma = \varnothing$, then $\tau = \varnothing \lhd \mu$, where $\mu$ is shorter than $\tau$. We have the theorem of HF $$ \vdash (x \in \varnothing \lhd \mu \leftrightarrow x \in \varnothing \lor x=\mu \leftrightarrow x=\mu), $$ i.e. $m=1$ and $\tau_1 = \mu$.

nodes.name: Case $\sigma\ne\varnothing$: elements of $\sigma$ plus $\mu$
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\sigma \neq \varnothing$. As $\sigma$ is shorter than $\tau$, there are $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_n \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $$ \vdash (x \in \sigma \leftrightarrow x=\sigma_1 \lor \ldots \lor x=\sigma_n) $$ Since $\vdash (x \in \tau \leftrightarrow x \in \sigma \lor x=\mu)$, we get $$ \vdash (x \in \tau \leftrightarrow x=\sigma_1 \lor \ldots \lor x=\sigma_n \lor x=\mu). $$ By inductive assumption, each $\sigma_i$ is shorter than $\sigma$, thus also shorter than $\tau$. Also, $\mu$ is shorter than $\tau$.

nodes.name: Proof of Distinct codes are provably distinct
nodes.statement: Say two constant terms $\sigma, \tau$ are \textit{identified} if $\vdash \sigma = \tau$. By Corollary \ref{cor:C.ne_of_not_eq}, either $\vdash \sigma = \tau$ or $\vdash \sigma \neq \tau$. It suffices to show that distinct constant terms in $\Gamma$ are never identified. Let $\sigma,\tau$ be distinct constant terms in $\Gamma$. We consider three cases: \textit{Case 1.} $\sigma, \tau \in \Gamma_0$. Suppose, without loss of generality, that $\tau$ is longer than $\sigma$ (see Definition \ref{def:C+C.length}). Then $\tau$ is obtained from $\sigma$ by several applications of the successor operation (see Definition \ref{def:succ}). But then $\vdash \sigma \in \tau$, and by Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}, $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are not identified. \textit{Case 2.} $\sigma \in \Gamma_0$ and $\tau \in \Gamma \setminus \Gamma_0$. We either have $\vdash \sigma = \varnothing$ or $\vdash \varnothing \in \sigma$. On the other hand, $\tau$ is an ordered pair. It is easily verified that every ordered pair is not equal to $\varnothing$ and does not contain $\varnothing$. Hence, $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are not identified. \textit{Case 3.} $\sigma, \tau \in \Gamma \setminus \Gamma_0$. We proceed by induction on the length of $\sigma$ to show that $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are not identified. The inductive assumption is that the desired implication holds if $\sigma, \tau$ are replaced by $\sigma^\prime, \tau^\prime$ where $\sigma^\prime$ is shorter than $\sigma$. Suppose $\sigma = \langle \sigma^\prime, \sigma^{\prime\prime} \rangle$ and $\tau = \langle \tau^\prime, \tau^{\prime\prime} \rangle$. As $\sigma,\tau$ are distinct, either $\sigma^\prime$ and $\tau^\prime$ are distinct or $\sigma^{\prime\prime}$ and $\tau^{\prime\prime}$ are distinct. Assume, without loss of generality, that $\sigma^\prime$ and $\tau^\prime$ are distinct. If $\sigma^\prime$ or $\tau^\prime$ is in $\Gamma_0$, then by Case 1 or Case 2, $\sigma^\prime$ and $\tau^\prime$ are not identified. Otherwise, if $\sigma^\prime, \tau^\prime \in \Gamma \setminus \Gamma_0$, then by the inductive assumption, $\sigma^\prime$ and $\tau^\prime$ are not identified. It follows that $\not\vdash \langle \sigma^\prime, \sigma^{\prime\prime} \rangle = \langle \tau^\prime, \tau^{\prime\prime} \rangle$, and hence $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are not identified.
