nodes.name: Subcase via Cases 1-2
nodes.statement: If $\sigma^\prime$ or $\tau^\prime$ is in $\Gamma_0$, then by Case 1 or Case 2, $\sigma^\prime$ and $\tau^\prime$ are not identified.

nodes.name: Subcase via the inductive assumption
nodes.statement: Otherwise, if $\sigma^\prime, \tau^\prime \in \Gamma \setminus \Gamma_0$, then by the inductive assumption, $\sigma^\prime$ and $\tau^\prime$ are not identified.

nodes.name: Hence the pairs are not identified
nodes.statement: It follows that $\not\vdash \langle \sigma^\prime, \sigma^{\prime\prime} \rangle = \langle \tau^\prime, \tau^{\prime\prime} \rangle$, and hence $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are not identified.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the pairs are not identified.

nodes.name: Ordered tuples
nodes.statement: In the following definitions, $\langle \sigma, \tau, \mu \rangle$ is a shorthand for the ordered pair $\langle \langle \sigma, \tau \rangle, \mu \rangle$, $\langle \sigma, \tau, \mu, \nu \rangle$ is a shorthand for $\langle \langle \sigma, \tau, \mu \rangle, \nu \rangle$, and so on.

nodes.name: Coding of symbols
nodes.statement: We begin by assigning to each symbol of the language a unique code denoted by $\ulcorner \cdot\urcorner$. In particular, these are the following constant terms belonging to $\Gamma$: $$ \begin{aligned} \ulcorner{\varnothing}\urcorner & =\varnothing, \\ \ulcorner{\in}\urcorner & =\langle \varnothing,\varnothing\rangle, \\ \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner & =\langle \varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing\rangle, \\ \ulcorner{=}\urcorner & =\langle \varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing\rangle, \\ \ulcorner{\lor}\urcorner & = \langle \varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing\rangle, \\ \ulcorner{\neg}\urcorner & = \langle \varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing\rangle, \\ \ulcorner{\exists}\urcorner & = \langle \varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing, \varnothing\rangle,\\ \ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner & = \varnothing \lhd \varnothing, \quad \ulcorner{x_2}\urcorner = \ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner,\quad\ldots\quad, \ulcorner{x_{k+1}}\urcorner = \ulcorner{x_k}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_k}\urcorner. \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Each symbol and variable gets a constant-term code in $\Gamma$ built from tuples of $\varnothing$.
nodes.label: def:Code.Symbol

nodes.name: Coding of terms
nodes.statement: The terms $\varnothing$ and $x_k$ have been coded already. The remaining case follows the inductive definition $$ \ulcorner{\sigma \lhd \tau}\urcorner = \langle\ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner \rangle. $$
nodes.label: def:Code.Term

nodes.name: Coding of formulas
nodes.statement: Given terms $\sigma, \tau$, the codes of atomic formulas are $$ \ulcorner{\sigma = \tau}\urcorner = \langle\ulcorner{=}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner \rangle \quad \text{and} \quad \ulcorner{\sigma \in \tau}\urcorner = \langle\ulcorner{\in}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner \rangle. $$ Non-atomic formulas follow the inductive definition $$ \begin{aligned} \ulcorner{\neg\varphi}\urcorner & = \langle\ulcorner{\neg}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner \rangle, \\ \ulcorner{\varphi \lor \psi}\urcorner & = \langle\ulcorner{\lor}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\psi}\urcorner \rangle, \\ \ulcorner{\exists x_k \varphi}\urcorner & = \langle\ulcorner{\exists}\urcorner, \ulcorner{x_k}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner \rangle. \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Codes of atomic and compound formulas as tuples headed by the code of the main symbol.
nodes.label: def:Code.Formula

nodes.name: Provability formula
nodes.statement: Specifically, we seek to identify an $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\operatorname{Pf}(x)$, referred to as the \textit{provability formula}, such that $$ \vdash \varphi \,\text{ if and only if } \vdash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner). $$

nodes.name: Strict Sigma-formula
nodes.statement: The class $\Sigma$ of \textit{strict $\Sigma$-formulas} is the smallest class of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas such that \begin{enumerate} \item The atomic formula $x_i \in x_j$ is in $\Sigma$ for all variables $x_i, x_j$. \item If $\varphi, \psi$ are in $\Sigma$, then so are $\varphi \lor \psi$ and $\varphi \land \psi$. \item If $\varphi$ is in $\Sigma$, then so are $\exists x_i \varphi$ and $\forall (x_i \in x_j) \varphi$ for all distinct variables $x_i, x_j$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Smallest class containing $x_i\in x_j$ and closed under $\lor,\land,\exists$ and bounded $\forall$.
nodes.label: def:IsInSSigma

nodes.name: Sigma-formula
nodes.statement: Say an $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$ is a \textit{$\Sigma$-formula} if there exists a strict $\Sigma$-formula $\psi$ such that $\vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$.
differentia: there exists a strict $\Sigma$-formula $\psi$ such that $\vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$
nodes.label: def:IsSigma

nodes.name: Basic formulas are Sigma-formulas
nodes.statement: The $\mathcal{L}$-formulas $x \subseteq y$, $x = y$, $z = x \lhd y$, $x=0$, $x\in 0$, $0 \in x$ and all atomic formulas are $\Sigma$-formulas.
conclusions: The $\mathcal{L}$-formulas $x \subseteq y$, $x = y$, $z = x \lhd y$, $x=0$, $x\in 0$, $0 \in x$ and all atomic formulas are $\Sigma$-formulas.
nodes.label: lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma

nodes.name: Proof of Basic formulas are Sigma-formulas
nodes.statement: The following are theorems of HF: \begin{enumerate} \item $x \subseteq y \leftrightarrow \forall (u \in x)[u \in y]$. \item $x = y \leftrightarrow x \subseteq y \land y \subseteq x$. \item $z = x \lhd y \leftrightarrow \forall(u \in z)[u \in x \lor u = y] \land (x \subseteq z) \land (y \in z)$. \item $x = 0 \leftrightarrow \forall (u \in x)[u \in u]$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty} and Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}). \item $x \in 0 \leftrightarrow x \in x$ (see Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}). \item $0 \in x \leftrightarrow \exists y (y = 0 \land y \in x)$. \end{enumerate} It follows from Definition \ref{def:IsInSSigma}.1, Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}.2 and Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}.3 that every atomic formula is a $\Sigma$-formula.

nodes.name: Six HF-theorems giving strict-$\Sigma$ equivalents
nodes.statement: The following are theorems of HF: \begin{enumerate} \item $x \subseteq y \leftrightarrow \forall (u \in x)[u \in y]$. \item $x = y \leftrightarrow x \subseteq y \land y \subseteq x$. \item $z = x \lhd y \leftrightarrow \forall(u \in z)[u \in x \lor u = y] \land (x \subseteq z) \land (y \in z)$. \item $x = 0 \leftrightarrow \forall (u \in x)[u \in u]$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty} and Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}). \item $x \in 0 \leftrightarrow x \in x$ (see Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}). \item $0 \in x \leftrightarrow \exists y (y = 0 \land y \in x)$.

nodes.name: Subset via bounded quantifier
nodes.statement: $x \subseteq y \leftrightarrow \forall (u \in x)[u \in y]$.

nodes.name: Equality via two inclusions
nodes.statement: $x = y \leftrightarrow x \subseteq y \land y \subseteq x$.

nodes.name: Adjunction via bounded formulas
nodes.statement: $z = x \lhd y \leftrightarrow \forall(u \in z)[u \in x \lor u = y] \land (x \subseteq z) \land (y \in z)$.

nodes.name: Emptiness via bounded formula
nodes.statement: $x = 0 \leftrightarrow \forall (u \in x)[u \in u]$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:notin_empty+mem_enlarge+mem_enlarge_empty} and Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}).

nodes.name: $x\in 0$ iff $x\in x$
nodes.statement: $x \in 0 \leftrightarrow x \in x$ (see Corollary \ref{cor:mem_irrefl}).

nodes.name: $0\in x$ via an existential
nodes.statement: $0 \in x \leftrightarrow \exists y (y = 0 \land y \in x)$.

nodes.name: Atomic formulas are $\Sigma$ by items 2-3
nodes.statement: It follows from Definition \ref{def:IsInSSigma}.1, Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}.2 and Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}.3 that every atomic formula is a $\Sigma$-formula.

nodes.name: Ord, Seq and LstSeq are Sigma-formulas
nodes.statement: Introduce the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\operatorname{LstSeq}(s,k,y)$, which means $\operatorname{Seq}(s,k)$ and $s$ terminates with $y$. The $\mathcal{L}$-formulas $\operatorname{Ord}(x)$, $\operatorname{Seq}(s,k)$ and $\operatorname{LstSeq}(s,k,y)$ are $\Sigma$-formulas.
assumptions: Introduce the $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\operatorname{LstSeq}(s,k,y)$, which means $\operatorname{Seq}(s,k)$ and $s$ terminates with $y$.
nodes.label: lem:Ord_isSigma+Seq_isSigma+LstSeq_isSigma

nodes.name: Proof of Ord, Seq and LstSeq are Sigma-formulas
nodes.statement: The following are theorems of HF: \begin{enumerate} \item $\operatorname{Ord}(x) \leftrightarrow \forall(y \in x)\{[y \subseteq x] \land \forall(z \in y)[z \subseteq y]\}$ (see Definition \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd} and Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}). \item $\operatorname{Seq}(s, k) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{Ord}(k) \land \varnothing \in k \land \forall(n \in k) \exists u[\langle n, u\rangle \in s] \land$ $\forall(y, z \in s) \exists(m, n \in k) \exists u \exists v[y=\langle m, u\rangle \land z=\langle n, v\rangle \land(m \neq n \lor u=v)]$. \item $\operatorname{LstSeq}(s, k, y) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{Seq}(s, k) \land \exists n(n \lhd n=k \land\langle n, y\rangle \in s)$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}). \end{enumerate} Observe that, in 2., $m \neq n$ is a $\Sigma$-formula if $m,n$ are ordinals, as it is equivalent to $m \in n \lor n \in m$ (see Corollary \ref{cor:IsOrd.exclusive_comparability+...+IsOrd.succ_inj}).

nodes.name: Strict-$\Sigma$ equivalents for Ord, Seq, LstSeq
nodes.statement: The following are theorems of HF: \begin{enumerate} \item $\operatorname{Ord}(x) \leftrightarrow \forall(y \in x)\{[y \subseteq x] \land \forall(z \in y)[z \subseteq y]\}$ (see Definition \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd} and Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}). \item $\operatorname{Seq}(s, k) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{Ord}(k) \land \varnothing \in k \land \forall(n \in k) \exists u[\langle n, u\rangle \in s] \land$ $\forall(y, z \in s) \exists(m, n \in k) \exists u \exists v[y=\langle m, u\rangle \land z=\langle n, v\rangle \land(m \neq n \lor u=v)]$. \item $\operatorname{LstSeq}(s, k, y) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{Seq}(s, k) \land \exists n(n \lhd n=k \land\langle n, y\rangle \in s)$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}).
nodes.statement_short: Strict-$\Sigma$ equivalents for Ord, Seq, LstSeq.

nodes.name: Ord via bounded quantifiers
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{Ord}(x) \leftrightarrow \forall(y \in x)\{[y \subseteq x] \land \forall(z \in y)[z \subseteq y]\}$ (see Definition \ref{def:IsTrans+IsOrd} and Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}).

nodes.name: Seq via bounded quantifiers
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{Seq}(s, k) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{Ord}(k) \land \varnothing \in k \land \forall(n \in k) \exists u[\langle n, u\rangle \in s] \land$ $\forall(y, z \in s) \exists(m, n \in k) \exists u \exists v[y=\langle m, u\rangle \land z=\langle n, v\rangle \land(m \neq n \lor u=v)]$.

nodes.name: LstSeq via Seq and an existential
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{LstSeq}(s, k, y) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{Seq}(s, k) \land \exists n(n \lhd n=k \land\langle n, y\rangle \in s)$ (see Lemma \ref{lem:subset_isSigma+...+empty_mem_isSigma}).
nodes.statement_short: LstSeq via Seq and an existential.

nodes.name: $m\neq n$ is $\Sigma$ for ordinals
nodes.statement: Observe that, in 2., $m \neq n$ is a $\Sigma$-formula if $m,n$ are ordinals, as it is equivalent to $m \in n \lor n \in m$ (see Corollary \ref{cor:IsOrd.exclusive_comparability+...+IsOrd.succ_inj}).

nodes.name: Sigma-sentence
nodes.statement: A \textit{$\Sigma$-sentence} is a $\Sigma$-formula that is a sentence, i.e. it has no free variables.

nodes.name: Sigma_lhd-formula and its length
nodes.statement: Say an $\mathcal{L}$-formula is a \textit{$\Sigma_{\lhd}$-formula} if it is made up of terms, the symbols ${\varnothing}$, ${=}$, ${\in}$, ${\lor}$, ${\land}$, ${\exists x_i}$, and ${\forall(x_i \in \tau)}$, where $\tau$ is any term that does not contain $x_i$. For a $\Sigma_{\lhd}$-formula $\alpha$, its length $\lambda(\alpha)$ is defined to be the total number of occurrences of the symbols $\lor$, $\land$, $\exists$, and $\forall$.
nodes.label: def:IsSigma_lhd

nodes.name: Sigma-completeness for the standard model
nodes.statement: If HF is consistent, then, for every $\Sigma$-sentence $\alpha$, $$ \vdash \alpha \,\text{ if and only if } \mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha. $$
nodes.statement_short: Assuming consistency, a $\Sigma$-sentence is provable iff it holds in $\mathfrak{S}$.
nodes.label: thm:stdModel.prf_iff_models

nodes.name: Proof of Sigma-completeness for the standard model
nodes.statement: By consistency, $\mathfrak{S}$ is a model of HF. Then, by soundness, it remains to show that for every $\Sigma$-sentence $\alpha$, $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha$ implies $\vdash \alpha$. Furthermore, since every strict $\Sigma$-sentence is a $\Sigma_{\lhd}$-sentence, it suffices to prove the result for every $\Sigma_{\lhd}$-sentence $\alpha$. We proceed by induction on the length $\lambda (\alpha)$. Suppose $\lambda(\alpha) = 0$. Then $\alpha$ must be of the form $\sigma \in \tau$ or $\sigma = \tau$ for some constant terms $\sigma, \tau$. The result follows directly from the definition of ${\in}$ and ${=}$ in $\mathfrak{S}$, i.e. in Definition \ref{def:stdModel}. Now assume $\lambda(\alpha) > 0$ and suppose the result holds for all $\Sigma_{\lhd}$-sentences of length less than $\lambda (\alpha)$. We consider the following cases: \begin{itemize} \item $\alpha$ is $\beta \lor \gamma$. By the inductive assumption, \begin{equation*} \mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha \rightarrow (\mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta \text{ or } \mathfrak{S} \vDash \gamma) \rightarrow (\vdash \beta \text{ or } \vdash \gamma) \rightarrow \vdash \beta \lor \gamma. \end{equation*} \item $\alpha$ is $\beta \land \gamma$. Analogous to the previous case. \item $\alpha$ is $\exists x \beta (x)$. If $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha$, then there exists a term $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau)$. Since $\lambda(\beta(\tau)) = \lambda(\beta) < \lambda(\alpha)$, it follows from the inductive assumption that $\vdash \beta(\tau)$, and hence $\vdash \exists x \beta (x)$. \item $\alpha$ is $\forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x)$, where $\tau$ is a term that does not contain $x$. Since there are no free variables in $\alpha$, $\tau$ must be a constant term. By Lemma \ref{lem:C.exists_finset_shorter_and_mem_iff_iSup}, there are $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_m \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $$ \vdash \forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x) \leftrightarrow \beta(\tau_1) \land \ldots \land \beta(\tau_m). $$ Since $\lambda(\beta(\tau_j)) = \lambda(\beta(x)) < \lambda(\alpha)$, it follows from the inductive assumption that \begin{equation*} \begin{split} & \mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha \rightarrow \mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau_1) \text{ and } \ldots \text{ and } \mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \\ &\vdash \beta(\tau_1) \text{ and } \ldots \text{ and } \vdash \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \vdash \beta(\tau_1) \land \ldots \land \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \vdash \forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x). \end{split} \end{equation*} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the length of $\Sigma_\lhd$-sentences, by cases on the outermost connective.

nodes.name: By soundness only the direction from truth in $\mathfrak{S}$ to provability remains
nodes.statement: By consistency, $\mathfrak{S}$ is a model of HF. Then, by soundness, it remains to show that for every $\Sigma$-sentence $\alpha$, $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha$ implies $\vdash \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: By soundness only the direction from truth in $\mathfrak{S}$ to provability remains.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\Sigma_\lhd$-sentences; induct on $\lambda$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since every strict $\Sigma$-sentence is a $\Sigma_{\lhd}$-sentence, it suffices to prove the result for every $\Sigma_{\lhd}$-sentence $\alpha$. We proceed by induction on the length $\lambda (\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Base case: atomic sentences, by definition of $\mathfrak{S}$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\lambda(\alpha) = 0$. Then $\alpha$ must be of the form $\sigma \in \tau$ or $\sigma = \tau$ for some constant terms $\sigma, \tau$. The result follows directly from the definition of ${\in}$ and ${=}$ in $\mathfrak{S}$, i.e. in Definition \ref{def:stdModel}.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: atomic sentences, by definition of $\mathfrak{S}$.

nodes.name: Inductive step by the outermost connective
nodes.statement: Now assume $\lambda(\alpha) > 0$ and suppose the result holds for all $\Sigma_{\lhd}$-sentences of length less than $\lambda (\alpha)$. We consider the following cases: \begin{itemize} \item $\alpha$ is $\beta \lor \gamma$. By the inductive assumption, \begin{equation*} \mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha \rightarrow (\mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta \text{ or } \mathfrak{S} \vDash \gamma) \rightarrow (\vdash \beta \text{ or } \vdash \gamma) \rightarrow \vdash \beta \lor \gamma. \end{equation*} \item $\alpha$ is $\beta \land \gamma$. Analogous to the previous case. \item $\alpha$ is $\exists x \beta (x)$. If $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha$, then there exists a term $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau)$. Since $\lambda(\beta(\tau)) = \lambda(\beta) < \lambda(\alpha)$, it follows from the inductive assumption that $\vdash \beta(\tau)$, and hence $\vdash \exists x \beta (x)$. \item $\alpha$ is $\forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x)$, where $\tau$ is a term that does not contain $x$. Since there are no free variables in $\alpha$, $\tau$ must be a constant term. By Lemma \ref{lem:C.exists_finset_shorter_and_mem_iff_iSup}, there are $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_m \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $$ \vdash \forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x) \leftrightarrow \beta(\tau_1) \land \ldots \land \beta(\tau_m). $$ Since $\lambda(\beta(\tau_j)) = \lambda(\beta(x)) < \lambda(\alpha)$, it follows from the inductive assumption that \begin{equation*} \begin{split} & \mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha \rightarrow \mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau_1) \text{ and } \ldots \text{ and } \mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \\ &\vdash \beta(\tau_1) \text{ and } \ldots \text{ and } \vdash \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \vdash \beta(\tau_1) \land \ldots \land \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \vdash \forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x). \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step by the outermost connective.

nodes.name: Disjunction
nodes.statement: $\alpha$ is $\beta \lor \gamma$. By the inductive assumption, \begin{equation*} \mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha \rightarrow (\mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta \text{ or } \mathfrak{S} \vDash \gamma) \rightarrow (\vdash \beta \text{ or } \vdash \gamma) \rightarrow \vdash \beta \lor \gamma. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Conjunction, analogous
nodes.statement: $\alpha$ is $\beta \land \gamma$. Analogous to the previous case.

nodes.name: Existential: witness by a constant term
nodes.statement: $\alpha$ is $\exists x \beta (x)$. If $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha$, then there exists a term $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau)$. Since $\lambda(\beta(\tau)) = \lambda(\beta) < \lambda(\alpha)$, it follows from the inductive assumption that $\vdash \beta(\tau)$, and hence $\vdash \exists x \beta (x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Existential: witness by a constant term.

nodes.name: Bounded universal: expand over finitely many elements via Lemma 5
nodes.statement: $\alpha$ is $\forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x)$, where $\tau$ is a term that does not contain $x$. Since there are no free variables in $\alpha$, $\tau$ must be a constant term. By Lemma \ref{lem:C.exists_finset_shorter_and_mem_iff_iSup}, there are $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_m \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $$ \vdash \forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x) \leftrightarrow \beta(\tau_1) \land \ldots \land \beta(\tau_m). $$ Since $\lambda(\beta(\tau_j)) = \lambda(\beta(x)) < \lambda(\alpha)$, it follows from the inductive assumption that \begin{equation*} \begin{split} & \mathfrak{S} \vDash \alpha \rightarrow \mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau_1) \text{ and } \ldots \text{ and } \mathfrak{S} \vDash \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \\ &\vdash \beta(\tau_1) \text{ and } \ldots \text{ and } \vdash \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \vdash \beta(\tau_1) \land \ldots \land \beta(\tau_m) \rightarrow \vdash \forall (x \in \tau) \beta(x). \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Bounded universal: expand over finitely many elements via Lemma 5.

nodes.name: Sigma-formulas for syntactic relations
nodes.statement: There exist 25 $\Sigma$-formulas, solely involving codes as arguments, that express certain relationships between variables, terms, and formulas.
conclusions: There exist 25 $\Sigma$-formulas, solely involving codes as arguments, that express certain relationships between variables, terms, and formulas.
nodes.label: lem:IsSigma.Relations

nodes.name: Proof of Sigma-formulas for syntactic relations
nodes.statement_short: List the 25 $\Sigma$-formulas with their meanings (written out in Swierczkowski).

nodes.name: Introduce abbreviations
nodes.statement: Introduce the following abbreviations of $\Sigma$-formulas:

nodes.name: Sigma-formula Var
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{Var}(x)$\\ Means: $x$ is the code of a variable.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula SeqTerm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{SeqTerm}(s,k,t)$\\ Means: $s$ is a sequence of length $k$ and $s$ terminates with the code $t$ of a term.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula Term
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{Term}(t)$\\ Means: $t$ is the code of a term.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula Const
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{Const}(t)$\\ Means: $t$ is the code of a constant term.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula NecSeqTerm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{NecSeqTerm}(s,k,t)$\\ Means: $s$ is a sequence of length $k$, $s$ terminates with the code $t$ of a term and all terms whose codes appear in $s$ are sub-terms of the term coded by $t$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula VarOccTerm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{VarOccTerm}(v,t)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $t$ codes a term and the variable coded by $v$ occurs in the term coded by $t$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula VarOccTerm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{VarOccTerm}(v,t)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $t$ codes a term and the variable coded by $v$ does not occur in the term coded by $t$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula At
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{At}(y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of an atomic formula.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula VarOccAt
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{VarOccAt}(v,y)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $y$ codes an atomic formula and the variable coded by $v$ occurs in the atomic formula coded by $y$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula VarNonOccAt
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{VarNonOccAt}(v,y)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $y$ codes an atomic formula and the variable coded by $v$ does not occur in the atomic formula coded by $y$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula MakeForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{MakeForm}(u,w,v,y)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable and if $u,w$ are codes of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas, then $y$ is the code of an $\mathcal{L}$-formula created from one or both $\mathcal{L}$-formulas coded by $u$, $w$ and possibly the variable coded by $v$ by a single application of ${\lor}$, ${\neg}$ or ${\exists}$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula SeqForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{SeqForm}(s,k,y)$\\ Means: $s$ is a sequence of length $k$ and $s$ terminates with the code $y$ of a $\mathcal{L}$-formula.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula Form
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{Form}(y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of an $\mathcal{L}$-formula.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula NonAt
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{NonAt}(y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of a non-atomic formula.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula VarTopForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{VarTopForm}(v,y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of an $\mathcal{L}$-formula beginning with $\exists x_i$, where $v$ codes the variable $x_i$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula SeqVarTopForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{SeqVarTopForm}(v,z,n,y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of an $\mathcal{L}$-formula and $z$ is a sequence of length $n$ showing how the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y$ is made up of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas beginning with $\exists x_i$ — where $v$ codes the variable $x_i$ — and of atomic formulas, by using ${\lor}$, ${\neg}$ and ${\exists x_j}$, where $j\neq i$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula NecSeqVarTopForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{NecSeqVarTopForm}(v,z,n,y)$\\ Means: as above, but additionally all $\mathcal{L}$-formulas whose codes appear in $z$ are sub-formulas of the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula VarOccFreeForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{VarOccFreeForm}(v,y)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $y$ codes an $\mathcal{L}$-formula and the variable coded by $v$ occurs freely in the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula VarNonOccFreeForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{VarNonOccFreeForm}(v,y)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $y$ codes an $\mathcal{L}$-formula and the variable coded by $v$ does not occur freely in the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula TermsSubsVarForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{TermsSubsVarForm}(t,v,y)$\\ Means: $t$ codes a term, $v$ codes a variable, $y$ codes an $\mathcal{L}$-formula, and the term coded by $t$ is a substitutable for the variable coded by $v$ in the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula SeqRepVarTermTerm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{SeqRepVarTermTerm}(s, s^\prime, k, v, t, u, u^\prime)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $t$ codes a term, $u$ and $u^\prime$ are coding terms and $s$ and $s^\prime$ are sequences of length $k$ such that $s$ terminates with $u$ and $s^\prime$ terminates with $u^\prime$ and the term coded by $u^\prime$ is obtained from that coded by $u$ by replacing each occurrence of the variable coded by $v$ by the term coded by $t$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula RepVarTermTerm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{RepVarTermTerm}(v, t, u, u^\prime)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $t$ codes a term, $u$ and $u^\prime$ code terms and replacing in the term coded by $u$ the variable coded by $v$, at all of its occurrences, by the term coded by $t$ one obtains the term coded by $u^\prime$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula RepVarTermAt
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{RepVarTermAt}(v, t, y, y^\prime)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $t$ codes a term, $y$ and $y^\prime$ are coding atomic formulas and replacing the variable coded by $v$ by the term coded by $t$, at all occurrences of this variable in the atomic formula coded by $y$, one obtains the atomic formula coded by $y^\prime$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula SeqRepVarTermForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{SeqRepVarTermForm}(s, s^\prime, k, v, t, y, y^\prime)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $t$ codes a term, $y$ and $y^\prime$ code $\mathcal{L}$-formulas and $s$ and $s^\prime$ are sequences of length $k$ such that $s$ terminates with $y$ and $s^\prime$ terminates with $y^\prime$ and the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y^\prime$ is obtained from that coded by $y$ by replacing each free occurrence of the variable coded by $v$ by the term coded by $t$.

nodes.name: Sigma-formula RepVarTermForm
nodes.statement: $\operatorname{RepVarTermForm}(v, t, y, y^\prime)$\\ Means: $v$ codes a variable, $t$ codes a term, $y$ and $y^\prime$ code atomic $\mathcal{L}$-formulas and replacing the variable coded by $v$ by the term coded by $t$, at all free occurrences of this variable in the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y$, one obtains the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y^\prime$.

nodes.name: The formula Pf
nodes.statement: There exist eight $\Sigma$-formulas, solely involving codes as arguments, that, together with the $\Sigma$-formulas in Lemma \ref{lem:IsSigma.Relations}, are sub-formulas of the $\Sigma$-formula $\operatorname{Pf}(x)$.
conclusions: There exist eight $\Sigma$-formulas, solely involving codes as arguments, that, together with the $\Sigma$-formulas in Lemma \ref{lem:IsSigma.Relations}, are sub-formulas of the $\Sigma$-formula $\operatorname{Pf}(x)$.
nodes.label: lem:IsSigma.Ax+...+IsSigma.Pf

nodes.name: Proof of The formula Pf
nodes.statement: Introduce the following abbreviations of $\Sigma$-formulas: \begin{enumerate} \item $\operatorname{Ax}(y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of the first axiom of HF, the second axiom of HF, or an equality axiom (see Definition \ref{def:Axioms} and Definition \ref{def:Equality.Axioms}). \item $\operatorname{Ind}(x)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of an instance of the induction scheme. \item $\operatorname{Sent}(x)$\\ Means: $x$ is the code of an $\mathcal{L}$-formula that is an instance of one of the five sentential axioms (see Definition \ref{def:Bool.Axioms}). \item $\operatorname{Spec}(x)$\\ Means: $x$ is the code of a specialisation axiom (see Definition \ref{def:Spec.Axiom}). \item $\operatorname{ModPon}(x,y,y^\prime)$\\ Means: If $x,y,y^\prime$ are codes of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas, then $y^\prime$ codes an $\mathcal{L}$-formula which follows from the $\mathcal{L}$-formulas coded by $x$ and $y$ by an application of the Modus Ponens rule (see Definition \ref{def:Prf.mp+Prf.subst+Prf.exists_intro}). \item $\operatorname{Subst}(y,y^\prime)$\\ Means: $y,y^\prime$ are codes of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas and the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y^\prime$ is obtained from that coded by $y$ by an application of the substitution rule. \item $\operatorname{ExIntro}(y, y^\prime)$\\ Means: $y,y^\prime$ are codes of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas and the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y^\prime$ is obtained from that coded by $y$ by an application of the $\exists$-introduction rule. \item $\operatorname{Prf}(s, k, y)$\\ Means: $s$ is a sequence of length $k$ of codes of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas such that the corresponding sequence of formulas is a proof of the $\mathcal{L}$-formula coded by $y$. \item $\operatorname{Pf}(y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of an $\mathcal{L}$-formula that is a theorem of HF. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: $\operatorname{Pf}(y)$\\ Means: $y$ is the code of an $\mathcal{L}$-formula that is a theorem of HF.

nodes.name: Proof formalisation condition
nodes.statement: If HF is consistent, then, for any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$, $$ \vdash \varphi \,\text{ if and only if } \vdash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner). $$
nodes.statement_short: Assuming consistency, $\varphi$ is provable iff $\operatorname{Pf}$ of its code is provable.
nodes.label: thm:prf_iff_prf_Pf_code

nodes.name: Proof of Proof formalisation condition
nodes.statement: Assume HF is consistent. First, suppose $\vdash \varphi$. Then there is a finite sequence of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas, $\varphi_{\varnothing}, \ldots, \varphi_p$, that forms a proof of $\varphi$. If $s = \{\langle l, \ulcorner{\varphi_l}\urcorner \rangle : l \in \operatorname{succ}(p) \}$, then $s \in \mathbb{S}$ (the domain of $\mathfrak{S}$, see Definition \ref{def:stdModel}) and $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \operatorname{Prf}(s, \operatorname{succ}(p), \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$, so that $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$. Since $\operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$ is a $\Sigma$-sentence, by Theorem \ref{thm:stdModel.prf_iff_models}, $\vdash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$. Now suppose $\vdash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$. Then, by Theorem \ref{thm:stdModel.prf_iff_models}, $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$. This means there exists a sequence $s \in \mathbb{S}$ of length $k$, where each $s_l$ codes some $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi_l$, so that $\varphi_{\operatorname{pred}(k)}$ equals $\varphi$ and the sequence $\varphi_{\varnothing}, \ldots, \varphi_{\operatorname{pred}(k)}$ is a proof of $\varphi$. Thus, $\vdash \varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions through Theorem 19 and the standard model.

nodes.name: Forward: code the proof as a sequence, then use Theorem 19
nodes.statement: Assume HF is consistent. First, suppose $\vdash \varphi$. Then there is a finite sequence of $\mathcal{L}$-formulas, $\varphi_{\varnothing}, \ldots, \varphi_p$, that forms a proof of $\varphi$. If $s = \{\langle l, \ulcorner{\varphi_l}\urcorner \rangle : l \in \operatorname{succ}(p) \}$, then $s \in \mathbb{S}$ (the domain of $\mathfrak{S}$, see Definition \ref{def:stdModel}) and $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \operatorname{Prf}(s, \operatorname{succ}(p), \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$, so that $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$. Since $\operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$ is a $\Sigma$-sentence, by Theorem \ref{thm:stdModel.prf_iff_models}, $\vdash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward: code the proof as a sequence, then use Theorem 19.

nodes.name: Backward: Theorem 19 gives truth in $\mathfrak{S}$, which decodes to a proof
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\vdash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$. Then, by Theorem \ref{thm:stdModel.prf_iff_models}, $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)$. This means there exists a sequence $s \in \mathbb{S}$ of length $k$, where each $s_l$ codes some $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi_l$, so that $\varphi_{\operatorname{pred}(k)}$ equals $\varphi$ and the sequence $\varphi_{\varnothing}, \ldots, \varphi_{\operatorname{pred}(k)}$ is a proof of $\varphi$. Thus, $\vdash \varphi$.

nodes.name: Coding function W on variables
nodes.statement: There exists a unary $p$-function $W$ such that, for any variable $x_i$, $$ \vdash W(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner) = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner. $$
conclusions: There exists a unary $p$-function $W$ such that
nodes.statement_short: A $p$-function $W$ maps each variable code to the code of that code.
nodes.label: lem:Code.exists_pFunc_forall_var_eq_code

nodes.name: Proof of Coding function W on variables
nodes.statement: Recall that the codes of variables are defined as $\ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner = \varnothing \lhd \varnothing, \quad \ulcorner{x_2}\urcorner = \ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner,\quad\ldots\quad, \ulcorner{x_{k+1}}\urcorner = \ulcorner{x_k}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_k}\urcorner$.\\ Define $W$ recursively on ordinals (see Definition \ref{def:Ord.pFuncRecursive}): $$ W(x) = \begin{cases} \varnothing & \text{if } x = \varnothing, \\ \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, W(\operatorname{pred}(x)), W(\operatorname{pred}(x)) \rangle & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ We apply induction on the index of the ordinal $x_i$, i.e. on its length (see Definition \ref{def:C+C.length}). First, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} W(\ulcorner(x_1)\urcorner) &= W(\operatorname{succ}(\varnothing)) = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, W(\varnothing), W(\varnothing) \rangle = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \varnothing \rangle \\ & = \ulcorner{\varnothing \lhd \varnothing}\urcorner = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner)}\urcorner. \end{split} \end{equation*} Now, suppose that $W(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner) = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner$. Then, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} W(\ulcorner{x_{i+1}}\urcorner) & = W(\operatorname{succ}(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)) = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, W(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner), W(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner) \rangle \\ & = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner, \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner \rangle = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_{i+1}}\urcorner)}\urcorner. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define $W$ by recursion on ordinals; induction on the variable index.

nodes.name: Recall the codes of variables
nodes.statement: Recall that the codes of variables are defined as $\ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner = \varnothing \lhd \varnothing, \quad \ulcorner{x_2}\urcorner = \ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner,\quad\ldots\quad, \ulcorner{x_{k+1}}\urcorner = \ulcorner{x_k}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_k}\urcorner$.

nodes.name: Define $W$ by recursion on ordinals
nodes.statement: Define $W$ recursively on ordinals (see Definition \ref{def:Ord.pFuncRecursive}): $$ W(x) = \begin{cases} \varnothing & \text{if } x = \varnothing, \\ \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, W(\operatorname{pred}(x)), W(\operatorname{pred}(x)) \rangle & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$

nodes.name: Base case $x_1$
nodes.statement: We apply induction on the index of the ordinal $x_i$, i.e. on its length (see Definition \ref{def:C+C.length}). First, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} W(\ulcorner(x_1)\urcorner) &= W(\operatorname{succ}(\varnothing)) = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, W(\varnothing), W(\varnothing) \rangle = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \varnothing \rangle \\ & = \ulcorner{\varnothing \lhd \varnothing}\urcorner = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_1}\urcorner)}\urcorner. \end{split} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Inductive step $x_i\to x_{i+1}$
nodes.statement: Now, suppose that $W(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner) = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner$. Then, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} W(\ulcorner{x_{i+1}}\urcorner) & = W(\operatorname{succ}(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)) = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, W(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner), W(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner) \rangle \\ & = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner, \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner \rangle = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner \lhd \ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner)}\urcorner = \ulcorner{(\ulcorner{x_{i+1}}\urcorner)}\urcorner. \end{split} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Coding function H
nodes.statement: There exists a unary $p$-function $H$ such that, for any code $\mu$, $$ \vdash H(\mu) = \ulcorner{\mu}\urcorner. $$
conclusions: There exists a unary $p$-function $H$ such that
nodes.statement_short: A $p$-function $H$ maps every code to its own code.
nodes.label: lem:Code.exists_pFunc_eq_code

nodes.name: Proof of Coding function H
nodes.statement: Recall the definition of an ordered pair: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \langle x, y \rangle & = \{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\} = \{\varnothing \lhd x, (\varnothing \lhd x) \lhd y\} \\ & = (\varnothing \lhd (\varnothing \lhd x)) \lhd ((\varnothing \lhd x) \lhd y). \end{split} \end{equation*} It follows that, for any terms $\sigma,\tau$, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \ulcorner {\langle \sigma, \tau \rangle} \urcorner & = \ulcorner {(\varnothing \lhd (\varnothing \lhd x)) \lhd ((\varnothing \lhd x) \lhd y)} \urcorner \\ & = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle\ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner \rangle \rangle, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner \rangle, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner \rangle \rangle. \end{split} \end{equation*} Let $t(x,y)$ be the term $\langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle\ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, x \rangle \rangle, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, x \rangle, y \rangle \rangle$. Then $t(\ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner) = \ulcorner {\langle \sigma, \tau \rangle} \urcorner$ for any terms $\sigma,\tau$. Now define $H$ recursively on rank (see Theorem \ref{thm:rank.exists_pFuncRecursive}): $$ H(x) = \begin{cases} W(x) & \text{if $x$ is an ordinal}, \\ t(H(u), H(v)) & \text{if } x = \langle u, v \rangle \text{ for some } u,v, \\ \varnothing & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ This definition makes sense as no ordered pair is an ordinal ($\varnothing \in x$ for every non-zero ordinal $x$, whereas $\varnothing \notin \langle u, v\rangle$ for all $u,v$), and $x = \langle u, v \rangle$ implies $u,v \in \operatorname{cl}(x)$. Suppose $\mu \in \Gamma$, i.e. $\mu$ is a code. If $\mu=\varnothing$ or $\mu$ is the code of a variable, then $H(\mu) = W(\mu) = \ulcorner{\mu}\urcorner$ by Lemma \ref{lem:Code.exists_pFunc_forall_var_eq_code}. All other terms $\mu \in \Gamma$ are built from $\varnothing$ and codes of variables by forming ordered pairs. Since for $\mu = \langle \sigma, \tau \rangle$ the terms $\sigma,\tau$ are shorter than $\mu$ (see Definition \ref{def:C+C.length}), we may proceed by induction on the length of $\mu$. Assume that $H(\sigma) = \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner$ and $H(\tau) = \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner$. Then, by the definition of $t(x,y)$, $$ \ulcorner{\mu}\urcorner = \ulcorner {\langle \sigma, \tau \rangle} \urcorner = t(\ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner) = t(H(\sigma), H(\tau)) = H(\mu), $$ Q.E.D.
nodes.statement_short: Define $H$ by recursion on rank via a pair-coding term $t$; induction on length.

nodes.name: Unfold ordered pairs in terms of $\lhd$
nodes.statement: Recall the definition of an ordered pair: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \langle x, y \rangle & = \{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\} = \{\varnothing \lhd x, (\varnothing \lhd x) \lhd y\} \\ & = (\varnothing \lhd (\varnothing \lhd x)) \lhd ((\varnothing \lhd x) \lhd y). \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Unfold ordered pairs in terms of $\lhd$.

nodes.name: Compute the code of a pair
nodes.statement: It follows that, for any terms $\sigma,\tau$, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \ulcorner {\langle \sigma, \tau \rangle} \urcorner & = \ulcorner {(\varnothing \lhd (\varnothing \lhd x)) \lhd ((\varnothing \lhd x) \lhd y)} \urcorner \\ & = \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle\ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner \rangle \rangle, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner \rangle, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner \rangle \rangle. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the code of a pair.

nodes.name: Define the term $t(x,y)$ computing pair codes
nodes.statement: Let $t(x,y)$ be the term $\langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle\ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, x \rangle \rangle, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \langle \ulcorner{\lhd}\urcorner, \varnothing, x \rangle, y \rangle \rangle$. Then $t(\ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner) = \ulcorner {\langle \sigma, \tau \rangle} \urcorner$ for any terms $\sigma,\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the term $t(x,y)$ computing pair codes.

nodes.name: Define $H$ by recursion on rank and check well-definedness
nodes.statement: Now define $H$ recursively on rank (see Theorem \ref{thm:rank.exists_pFuncRecursive}): $$ H(x) = \begin{cases} W(x) & \text{if $x$ is an ordinal}, \\ t(H(u), H(v)) & \text{if } x = \langle u, v \rangle \text{ for some } u,v, \\ \varnothing & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ This definition makes sense as no ordered pair is an ordinal ($\varnothing \in x$ for every non-zero ordinal $x$, whereas $\varnothing \notin \langle u, v\rangle$ for all $u,v$), and $x = \langle u, v \rangle$ implies $u,v \in \operatorname{cl}(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $H$ by recursion on rank and check well-definedness.

nodes.name: Base: $\varnothing$ and variable codes via $W$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mu \in \Gamma$, i.e. $\mu$ is a code. If $\mu=\varnothing$ or $\mu$ is the code of a variable, then $H(\mu) = W(\mu) = \ulcorner{\mu}\urcorner$ by Lemma \ref{lem:Code.exists_pFunc_forall_var_eq_code}.

nodes.name: Pairs by induction on length using $t$
nodes.statement: All other terms $\mu \in \Gamma$ are built from $\varnothing$ and codes of variables by forming ordered pairs. Since for $\mu = \langle \sigma, \tau \rangle$ the terms $\sigma,\tau$ are shorter than $\mu$ (see Definition \ref{def:C+C.length}), we may proceed by induction on the length of $\mu$. Assume that $H(\sigma) = \ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner$ and $H(\tau) = \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner$. Then, by the definition of $t(x,y)$, $$ \ulcorner{\mu}\urcorner = \ulcorner {\langle \sigma, \tau \rangle} \urcorner = t(\ulcorner{\sigma}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner) = t(H(\sigma), H(\tau)) = H(\mu), $$ Q.E.D.
nodes.statement_short: Pairs by induction on length using $t$.

nodes.name: The replacement function
nodes.statement: There exists a ternary $p$-function, denoted by $\operatorname{REPL}$, such that $$ \vdash \operatorname{REPL}(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner, \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner) = \ulcorner{\varphi(x_i/\tau)}\urcorner $$ for every variable $x_i$, term $\tau$ and $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi$, where $\varphi(x_i/\tau)$ results from replacing each free occurrence of $x_i$ in $\varphi$ by $\tau$.
conclusions: There exists a ternary $p$-function, denoted by $\operatorname{REPL}$, such that
nodes.statement_short: A $p$-function REPL computes, on codes, the code of the substitution $\varphi(x_i/\tau)$.
nodes.label: lem:Code.exists_repl

nodes.name: Proof of The replacement function
nodes.statement: As the defining $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi(v,t,y,y^\prime)$ for $\operatorname{REPL}$ choose: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} & [(\exists!z)\operatorname{RepVarTermForm}(v,t,y,z) \land \operatorname{RepVarTermForm}(v,t,y,y^\prime)] \lor \\ & [\not (\exists!z)\operatorname{RepVarTermForm}(v,t,y,z) \land y^\prime = 0]. \end{split} \end{equation*} Then it is clear that $(\exists!y^\prime)\varphi(v,t,y,y^\prime)$. By the meaning of the $\Sigma$-formula $\operatorname{REPL}$, as described in \ref{lem:IsSigma.Relations}, the result follows. For the precise details, including the written-out $\Sigma$-formula $\operatorname{REPL}$, the reader is referred to Sections 3 and 5 of \cite{swierczkowski2003finite}.
nodes.statement_short: Define REPL from RepVarTermForm; details in Swierczkowski.

nodes.name: Choose the defining formula; it is functional
nodes.statement: As the defining $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi(v,t,y,y^\prime)$ for $\operatorname{REPL}$ choose: \begin{equation*} \begin{split} & [(\exists!z)\operatorname{RepVarTermForm}(v,t,y,z) \land \operatorname{RepVarTermForm}(v,t,y,y^\prime)] \lor \\ & [\not (\exists!z)\operatorname{RepVarTermForm}(v,t,y,z) \land y^\prime = 0]. \end{split} \end{equation*} Then it is clear that $(\exists!y^\prime)\varphi(v,t,y,y^\prime)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the defining formula; it is functional.

nodes.name: Result follows from the meaning of RepVarTermForm (details in Swierczkowski)
nodes.statement: By the meaning of the $\Sigma$-formula $\operatorname{REPL}$, as described in \ref{lem:IsSigma.Relations}, the result follows. For the precise details, including the written-out $\Sigma$-formula $\operatorname{REPL}$, the reader is referred to Sections 3 and 5 of \cite{swierczkowski2003finite}.
nodes.statement_short: Result follows from the meaning of RepVarTermForm (details in Swierczkowski).

nodes.name: Diagonalisation function K
nodes.statement: For every variable $x_i$, there exists a unary $p$-function $K$ such that, for any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\varphi(x_i)$, $$ \vdash K (\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner) = \ulcorner{\varphi(\ulcorner {\varphi} \urcorner)}\urcorner. $$
conclusions: there exists a unary $p$-function $K$ such that
nodes.statement_short: A $p$-function $K$ sends $\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner$ to the code of $\varphi$ applied to its own code.
nodes.label: lem:Code.exists_pFunc_forall_form_eq_code_form

nodes.name: Proof of Diagonalisation function K
nodes.statement: First, note that the composite of $p$-functions is a $p$-function. Now put $$ K(x) = \operatorname{REPL}(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner, H(x), x). $$ Let $\tau = \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner$. Then, by \ref{lem:Code.exists_pFunc_eq_code}, $\ulcorner{\tau}\urcorner = H (\tau)$ and furthermore, by \ref{lem:Code.exists_repl}, $$ \vdash \operatorname{REPL}(\ulcorner{x_i}\urcorner, H(\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner), \ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner) = \ulcorner{\varphi(\ulcorner {\varphi} \urcorner)}\urcorner, $$ i.e. $\vdash K (\ulcorner{\varphi}\urcorner)= \ulcorner{\varphi(\ulcorner {\varphi} \urcorner)}\urcorner$.

nodes.statement: For any $\mathcal{L}$-formula $\alpha$ with one free variable, there exists a sentence $\delta$ such that $$ \vdash \delta \leftrightarrow \alpha(\ulcorner{\delta}\urcorner). $$

nodes.name: Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem
nodes.statement: If HF is consistent, then there exists a sentence $\delta$ such that neither $\vdash \delta$ nor $\vdash \neg \delta$. Furthermore, $\mathfrak{S} \vDash \delta$.
conclusions: there exists a sentence $\delta$ such that neither $\vdash \delta$ nor $\vdash \neg \delta$.

nodes.name: Proof of Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Apply the diagonal lemma to $\neg\operatorname{Pf}$; each alternative contradicts consistency.

nodes.name: $\vdash\delta$ contradicts consistency
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vdash \delta$. Then, by Theorem \ref{thm:prf_iff_prf_Pf_code}, $\vdash \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\delta}\urcorner)$. On the other hand, by \ref{eq:diag}, $\vdash \neg \operatorname{Pf}(\ulcorner{\delta}\urcorner)$. This contradicts the assumption of consistency.

nodes.name: $\vdash\neg\delta$ contradicts consistency
